items.title: feat(lynx-observability): Memory.query() — real engine memory numbers
items.body:
Part of #953. Docs issue: signalxjs/signalxjs.github.io#594.

Gives `@sigx/lynx-observability` its first resource telemetry, and the repo its first JS-side memory instrumentation. `Memory.query()` returns a process-global reading covering every LynxView: `totalBytes` against the app's own `appBytes`, the element tree as `elementBytes` **and** `elementNodeCount`, platform UI bytes, both runtime heaps, and a per-instance breakdown sorted by size. That element-bytes-against-node-count pairing is the signal #603 and #606 have been missing — it turns "the screen went blank" into "we're mounting 12,000 nodes".

## Why this needs native code

The package's first. The reading cannot be had from JS: Lynx does emit a `memory` `PerformanceEntry`, but `memory_monitor.cc` sends it with `kEventTypePlatform` only, so it reaches native observers and never the background or main-thread JS runtimes. `MemoryUsageEntry` is nonetheless declared in `@lynx-js/types`, which makes `lynx.performance.createObserver(…).observe(['memory'])` type-check, look right in an editor, and return silence on device. Confirmed on device, not just read off the source.

Two things made it cheaper than the issue assumed:

- **No engine setting is required.** `enable_memory_monitor` gates only the passive entry stream; `LynxTemplateRender.registerMemoryUsageFetcherIfNeeded()` registers unconditionally. The iOS log line `new MemoryMonitor … Enable:false` during the verification run confirms the query works with the monitor off — so no `LynxEnv` plumbing and no host-template change.
- **The headers are public.** `LynxMemoryUsageQuery.h` and `LynxMemoryUsageResult.h` are both in the `Lynx/Framework` subspec's `public_header_files` and appear in `Lynx-umbrella.h`, so plain `import Lynx` reaches them — no bridging header, no ObjC shim.

## Shape of the API

```ts
const m = await Memory.query();              // or { timeoutMs }
m.totalBytes; m.elementNodeCount; m.instances[0].url;
Memory.isAvailable();                        // C2 — is the native module linked
```

A `'timeout'` status is a **partial result, not an error** — `query()` resolves, and `completedInstanceCount` against `expectedInstanceCount` says how much of the reading arrived. Getting this wrong reads as a memory drop that never happened, so it's called out in the type docs, the README, and the demo screen.

Both platforms send every number as a double so one JS normalizer serves both, and the collection-status enum is stringified at the native boundary so JS never sees a magic int and a future enum member degrades to `'unknown'`. Both callbacks are guarded against a double invoke: a Lynx `Callback` / `LynxCallbackBlock` fired twice takes the bridge down rather than just the call, and "the timeout fires, then the slow instance completes" is exactly the shape that would do it.

## Device verification — release builds, both platforms

Per #953's own measurement discipline, everything below is from `--release` builds. No dev-build numbers are quoted.

**Android** (physical Pixel, release APK, embedded bundle):

```
status completed · took 2ms of 2000ms · 2/2 instance(s)
lynx 34.8 MB of app 221.2 MB · 15.7%
elements 0.9 MB over 909 node(s) · views 0.0 MB
runtime MT 8.0 MB · BG 25.9 MB
Instances (2): #1 19.9 MB / 680 nodes · #0 14.9 MB / 229 nodes
```

**iOS** (iPhone 13 mini simulator, iOS 26, release build):

```
status completed · took 4ms of 2000ms · 1/1 instance(s)
lynx 4.9 MB of app 98.7 MB · 5.0%
elements 0.5 MB over 549 node(s) · views 0.2 MB
runtime MT 4.2 MB · BG 0.0 MB
Instances (1): #0 …/showcase.app/main.lynx.bundle · 4.9 MB / 549 nodes
```

**The failure path too**, not just the happy one: the demo's "Force a timeout" button (`timeoutMs: 1`) resolves on both platforms with `collectionStatus: 'timeout'` and `0/2` instances, and the screen renders the partial-result warning rather than an error.

The per-instance sum matches `totalBytes` exactly on Android (19.9 + 14.9 = 34.8), which is the arithmetic check worth having.

**Platform asymmetries, documented rather than papered over.** Android reports no `viewBytes`, iOS reports no `backgroundThreadRuntimeBytes`, and only iOS fills in `url`. `totalBytes`, `elementBytes` and `elementNodeCount` — the three that matter for the diagnosis this exists for — are solid on both. The README carries the table and the "compare a platform against itself, not against the other one" rule.

## Also here

- **A showcase screen** (`Native modules → Memory`), which clears the standing D7.6 "no showcase screen" finding on #896. It covers the failure paths, not just the happy one: the forced timeout, the unlinked-module throw, and an `isAvailable()`-gated banner so it renders on web.
- **The README is rewritten to the C11 template.** Adding `signalx-module.json` flips `isNativeModule` on in `scripts/check-api-conventions.mjs`, which then requires a `## Web` section — and Install/Usage/API/Gotchas/License were all missing too, so this PR owns them. `pnpm check:conventions` and `pnpm check:manifests` are both green with **no baseline entry added**; `lynx-observability` stays at zero known violations.
- Two pre-existing packaging gaps fixed while here: `sideEffects` (only `./dist/install.js` has any) and a `test` script.

**Breaking-ish for consumers:** installing this package changes your OTA runtime fingerprint, because it adds native sources. Re-run `sigx prebuild`, cut a store release, and republish your update bundles. Requires Lynx ≥ 4.0.1.

## Tests

25 new. The normalization cases aren't padding — these values land in log records and dashboards, so a `NaN` or a stray `-1` travels further than a bad return value normally would. Covered: the literal module/method reaching `callAsync` (C12 reads it textually), `timeoutMs` forwarding, `instanceId: -1 → null`, payload-arriving-as-a-JSON-string (#342), non-finite numbers, an unknown status, malformed instance rows, the `{ error }` envelope becoming a prefixed `SigxError` (C4/C10), and the unlinked-module throw (C3). Plus a public-surface freeze test that pins the barrel, the signatures, `isAvailable`'s synchronicity (C2), and native-vs-web surface parity.

Both regression guards were proved by breaking the code and watching them fail: reverting the `-1 → null` normalization and removing the JSON-string branch each turn exactly one test red.

## Follow-ups

`viewDetail` is deliberately not surfaced — the engine reports per-view-class records per instance, but the shape isn't pinned across platforms and the aggregate plus `elementNodeCount` is what the diagnosis needs. Noted in Gotchas, with a follow-up to file if demand appears. The periodic reporter and the background-thread `PerformanceObserver` wrapper are the next PR on #953.

items.title: feat(stats): honest memory numbers, per-subprocess splitting, and scrubbable resource graphs
items.body:
## What this is

Veld's per-node resource monitoring reported a memory figure that was **wrong**, not merely coarse, and offered no detail behind it. This makes the number honest and then builds the detailed view on top: memory split by page class, CPU and memory split by subprocess, a `veld stats` CLI, and a scrubbable chart in the management UI that switches between memory and CPU.

## Root cause of the wrong number

The old aggregate summed **RSS** over a node's process tree. RSS counts every resident page, including pages *shared between the processes being summed* — the shared libc, the shared Node runtime, every copy-on-write page inherited at fork. So a five-process `npm run dev` reported far more than it occupied, and the error grew with the tree.

The headline figure is now the tree's **footprint**:

| platform | source | figure |
|---|---|---|
| Linux | `/proc/<pid>/smaps_rollup` | `Pss` — each shared page divided by the number of processes mapping it, so a tree sum is honest |
| macOS | `proc_pid_rusage(RUSAGE_INFO_V4)` | `ri_phys_footprint` — the number Activity Monitor shows |

Both degrade to RSS when the detailed source is unreadable, so a graph never goes blank.

## What's new

- **Page-class split** where the platform can: private dirty (the heap — what grows when a service leaks), private clean, shared dirty, shared clean, swap, wired. macOS has no unprivileged equivalent, so those fields are **absent rather than guessed**, and every surface renders an absent class as unavailable — never as zero.
- **Per-subprocess rows.** Each sample also stores one row per process (pid, parent, depth, name, argv, CPU, cumulative CPU seconds, full breakdown) in its own table rather than a JSON blob, so "graph this one child over the last hour" is a `WHERE pid = ?` with an index behind it.
- **`veld stats`** — `--processes`, `--history --window 15m`, `--cpu`, `--memory <metric>`, `--all-metrics`, `--json`. `veld status` stays compact; its `MEM` column now shows footprint.
- **Scrubbable chart in the UI.** Click a node's stats to expand: window picker (5m→24h), Memory | CPU, and three split modes — total, by page class, by subprocess — over the live process table. Hand-rolled SVG, because this UI is inlined into the daemon binary and a charting library would be a charting library in `veld-daemon`.
- **History bucketed in SQL** at query time (`/api/stats/history`), so payload size follows requested resolution rather than run uptime.

## Design rules worth knowing before reviewing

**An absent value is never zero.** If any process in a tree — or any sample in a bucket — cannot report a page class, the total reports *none*. Coercing the gap to zero would present a partial breakdown as a complete one that happens to be too small, which is the exact error a resource graph must not make. This rule is enforced in `MemoryBreakdown::add`, in SQL (`CASE WHEN COUNT(x) = COUNT(*) THEN AVG(x) END`), and in the chart's drawability rule.

**A gap is a gap.** Buckets with no samples are omitted, not zero-filled: "the daemon wasn't sampling" and "the node used no memory" must not render identically, so the chart breaks the line and the terminal sparkline leaves a hole.

**Migration 7** adds the breakdown columns to `node_stats` and creates `node_process_stats`. The new columns are nullable with no default deliberately — a pre-v7 row genuinely has no footprint reading, and `NULL` is how a reader tells that from a real zero. `footprint` falls back to `memory_bytes` at read time so old samples keep plotting instead of dropping to zero mid-graph. Purely additive: no `ALTER` or `DROP` of anything existing.

## Retention

Node totals 24h (was 6h), per-process rows 2h — they outnumber the aggregates by the tree size, and a subprocess breakdown answers "what is happening", not "what happened yesterday". Both horizons have **one definition** in `veld_core::stats` and are served by the API, so the GC, the window clamp and the UI's presets cannot drift apart.

Two daemon-environment escape hatches, `VELD_STATS_MEMORY_DETAIL=off` and `VELD_STATS_CMDLINE=off`. Note these must be set where a launchd/systemd service can see them — a shell `export` does not reach the daemon; `skills/veld/SKILL.md` documents the exact commands.

## Test evidence

```
cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets   0 warnings
cargo clippy --workspace -- -D warnings  clean (as CI runs it)
cargo fmt --all --check                  clean
cargo test --workspace                   680 passed, 3 ignored
(ui) npm run typecheck                   clean
(ui) npm test                            240 passed
tests/validate-schema.sh                 15 passed, 0 failed
```

Beyond the suites, verified by execution:

- **The Linux paths, on Linux.** This was developed on macOS, so `smaps_rollup` parsing, the `/proc/<pid>/stat` field offsets and `_SC_CLK_TCK` had never run. I extracted the parsers as pure functions and ran them in Docker on real Linux — 7/7, including reading this process's own `/proc/self/smaps_rollup` and asserting the page-class split is present.
- **The pre-v7 upgrade path**, by writing rows naming only the columns a pre-v7 binary knew and reading them back through both the Rust and SQL fallbacks.
- **The live HTTP API** on an isolated daemon: 400 without a project scope, 404 for an untracked project, window clamped to retention, points capped, `serde(flatten)` keys colliding with nothing, and no CORS headers (so the same-origin policy blocks cross-origin reads, matching the pre-existing `/api/stats`).
- **The CLI's gap rendering**, against a seeded 9-minute hole in a 15-minute window — it renders as a hole.
- **`veld status` and `veld stats` agree** on the same live node (389 MB / 389 MB), reading the same field via the same query.

## Review

Ran the autonomous multi-angle loop in `docs/agentic-review.md` at standard depth; the SQLite migration and daemon HTTP API tripped §3.3, forcing opus on angles 3 and 7 and a round cap of 5. **4 rounds, 12 subagent spawns (6 opus / 6 sonnet), 33 findings** — 1 critical, 9 major, the rest medium/minor. Every 🔴/🟠 was verified by hand before any code changed.

The most useful catches were the ones I'd have shipped:

- **The by-process chart blanked whenever any child was absent from a bucket** — routine, since dev-server children restart. My seeded fixture happened to give every PID a value in every bucket, which is exactly why I missed it.
- **A transient probe failure closed the by-type view.** One short-lived child failing its `smaps` read poisoned the newest bucket's classes, which dropped every class from the picker, which reset the reader's chosen metric and kicked them out of the split view — and never restored it.
- **Both escape hatches were unreachable.** They're read from the sampler's environment, but the sampler lives in a launchd/systemd service that inherits no shell environment — the exact asymmetry AGENTS.md already documents for daemon `PATH`. `VELD_STATS_CMDLINE=off`, a privacy control, silently did nothing.
- **Three of my own fixes introduced fresh defects**, which is the argument for the later rounds existing at all: an absence gate applied to Rust but not its TypeScript mirror; a gate moved to preserve CPU time that left the expensive read running and discarded (demoting a performance escape hatch to a display-only one); and a presence rule made metric-aware but not dimension-aware, which resurrected the first bug on a new path.

One concern — when a stacked chart may draw an index — produced a defect in **four consecutive passes**, each a patch on the previous patch. The final change stops patching: the chart-level policy is deleted and each series carries `absent: "did-not-exist" | "unmeasurable"`, set where its nulls are produced. `TimeSeriesChart` no longer accepts a policy, so no caller can pass the wrong one, and the field is required, so a new series can't be added without deciding.

## Known follow-ups (deliberately not in this PR)

- `veld status --json` omits its `stats` map entirely when empty (`skip_serializing_if`), the same agent-facing trap fixed here for `processes` — but it's **pre-existing**, so changing it alters a shipped wire shape beyond this change's scope.
- `output.rs`'s `fmt_bytes` and the UI's `fmtBytes` differ by one decimal at MB/GB. Both predate this change; the false parity claim in the doc is corrected, aligning the formats is separate.
- `port::tests::test_reservation_holds_port` flakes under full parallel load (untouched file, passes 5/5 in isolation).
- Two pre-existing unresolved intra-doc links in `presets.rs` and `user_path.rs`.
- Per-process rows can't distinguish "this process didn't exist" from "its probe failed" on the wire, so a by-process page-class stack takes the conservative rule. A per-row flag would let it be exact.

## Reviewer scope notes

- **Stakes-elevated paths:** migration 7 (`crates/veld-core/src/db/mod.rs`), the new HTTP endpoint (`management.rs`), and the `unsafe` `proc_pid_rusage` block (`procmem.rs`) — the last was verified sound against the real libc source: `rusage_info_t` is `void *`, the cast reproduces the C call, `RUSAGE_INFO_V4` matches the struct, the buffer is full-size so the kernel cannot overrun it, and every field is `u64`/`[u8;16]` so `mem::zeroed()` is valid.
- **argv is a new data class.** Process command lines are now stored (0600 DB, 2h) and served from the daemon's localhost API. No boundary opens that `/api/logs` doesn't already cross, and React escapes it at every render position, but it's the thing to push back on if you disagree — hence `VELD_STATS_CMDLINE=off`.
- **Docs checklist:** README, `skills/veld/SKILL.md`, `website/index.html` + `llms-full.txt` updated. `docs/configuration.md`, both JSON schemas and `docs/migrating-to-v3.md` are genuinely exempt — this adds no config fields.

items.title: Offline-profiler benchmark scripts + measured Gate 1 numbers (memory ✓, throughput ✓, thermal documented)
items.body:
### Summary

Closes the M2 milestone of the ADTC 2026 Gate 1 track: this PR turns "we built an offline binder" into "we can **prove** its contest numbers". It adds a reproducible measurement toolkit (offline proof, profiler smoke, thread matrix, thermal soak), ships the measured results in `BENCHMARKS.md`, and freezes the empirically-best server configuration.

Every number in this PR was **measured on this build laptop** (Intel i7-8650U · 23.3 GB RAM · Ubuntu 22.04 · no GPU) — nothing invented. The application code is unchanged from Gate 1 (merged in #1).

### What changed (13 files: 5 modified, 8 new)

**New measurement scripts**
| Script | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `scripts/offline_check.sh` | Binder offline proof: credit / SOCA refuse / stock asserts + ledger flip-and-restore bind proof; re-runs asks inside `unshare -n` when available (airplane-mode proof) |
| `scripts/run_profiler_smoke.sh` | `adtc-profiler` participant mode → `benchmarks/raw/submission.json` + auto-generated `benchmarks/submission.summary.md`; optional `--full` accuracy pass |
| `scripts/thread_matrix.sh` | `llama-bench` thread bake-off (`-t 2,3,4,6,8`) with package-temp sampling after each run |
| `scripts/thermal_soak.sh` | 10-min sustained-generation soak (5 s sampling) → CSV + PASS/FAIL verdict; **enforces single-server measurement** (pre-flight port/process guard + in-loop contamination detection + FAIL on <100 % HTTP) |

**Config freeze**
- `scripts/start_llama_server.sh` — `THREADS=3` frozen from the thread matrix (`-t 3` = 17.94 tg_tps; `-t 8` collapsed TPS *and* hit 85 °C). Still overridable via env for experiments.

**Measured artifacts + docs**
- `BENCHMARKS.md` — all measured tables with run provenance; raw dumps stay gitignored under `benchmarks/raw/`
- `benchmarks/README.md`, `benchmarks/submission.summary.md`, `benchmarks/.gitignore`
- `REPORT.md`, `README.md`, `docs/CODE_WALKTHROUGH.md`, `docs/README.md` — updated to match measured reality

### Measured numbers (all from this laptop)

**Profiler smoke** (2026-08-04, `--skip-accuracy`)

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| Peak RSS | **1825.6 MB** (≪ 5.5 GB self-limit, ≪ 7 GB DQ) |
| Generation TPS | **14.73 tok/s** (reference ≈ 15) |
| TTFT | 9865.49 ms |
| Core temp peak | 100.0 °C — throttled ⚠️ |

**Thread matrix** (2026-08-05, `llama-bench -t 2,3,4,6,8`)

| threads | tg_tps | pp_tps | temp | note |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| 2 | 14.96 | 45.79 | 76 °C | ok |
| **3** | **17.94** | 63.73 | 77 °C | **frozen default** |
| 4 | 16.57 | 62.52 | 76 °C | ok |
| 6 | 16.32 | 62.20 | 79 °C | ok |
| 8 | 7.53 | 59.74 | **85 °C** | hot — collapsed TPS |

**Thermal soak** (2026-08-06, `THREADS=3`, `ctx=2048`, single server, 10 min)

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| Samples / HTTP success | 75 / **100 %** |
| Temp mean | **78.1 °C** |
| Temp peak | **97.0 °C** (at +297 s) |
| ≥ 85 °C samples | 9/75 (12 %) |
| Verdict | **FAIL** on this 2018-era laptop |

### Thermal mitigation plan (honest status)

- Steady state is comfortable (mean 78 °C, no runaway) — the failure is **intermittent bursts**, same pattern as the 100 °C profiler smoke.
- **M2 is not closed on thermal** for this host. Ordered mitigations:
  1. Re-soak at `THREADS=2` (matrix measured 76 °C / 14.96 tg_tps there — ~17 % TPS cost for thermal headroom)
  2. `CTX=1024` + shorter `max_tokens` on the soak payload
  3. P_thermal is decided on the **official eval machine** (i5 12th-gen / Ryzen 5), which cools differently — record that run separately when available
- Memory ✓ and throughput ✓ buckets are measured and safe; thermal is the only open item and it is **documented, not hidden**.

### Validation

- `PYTHONPATH=. pytest tests/ -q` → **19 passed** (Gate 1 suite unchanged)
- `ruff check app tests scripts` → clean
- `bash -n` on all 7 scripts → clean
- `bash scripts/offline_check.sh` → **PASS** (incl. ledger flip + restore)
- `bash scripts/smoke_narrate.sh` → **PASS** end-to-end: `source: binder+llm`, LLM restated exact binder figures (8410 XAF / 410 over / max 2 crates) — zero hallucination, `message` authoritative
- Negative test: soak pre-flight correctly **refuses** while another server runs (exit 1)

items.title: Added commentary
items.body:
What's in v1.0.1
Intensively commented source — every file in src/ plus train_demo.py now explains the design contract, the math behind each backward line, numerical-stability choices, why gradients accumulate with +=, why v isn't rotated by RoPE, why np.add.at is required for embeddings, the online-softmax invariants, etc. Rewritten README — per-file repo map, run instructions, design decisions, updated results table, and a changelog documenting all three review fixes. New report/how_it_works.md — a detailed engineering report: the module contract, forward pass step by step, the five reusable backward rules, the FlashAttention recompute trade, optimizer mechanics, verification methodology, memory numbers, and honest limitations (complementing your math-focused derivations.md). Regenerated artifacts — fresh import_audit.txt, results.csv, benchmark.png, loss_curve.png, and sample.txt from the fixed code (training still converges: loss 3.95 → 0.084, corpus reproduced verbatim).

items.title: release: 0.7.0 — dgrad kernel + batched LoRA delta
items.body:
Version bump and CHANGELOG for the two training-lane merges, #35 and #36.

Both per-expert Python loops in the training lane are gone. Each hid the other — removing one alone buys little, because whichever remains dominates:

| E=256 step (A2000, 512 tokens, top_k 8) | | |
|---|---|---|
| stock | 403.7 ms | 72 MB |
| delta batching only (#35) | 136.5 ms | 108 MB |
| dgrad only (#36) | 316.1 ms | 98 MB |
| **both** | **26.5 ms (~15x)** | **134 MB** |

For scale, experts4bit-qlora's kernel-free `enable_batched_train` runs the same step in 25.0 ms at **417 MB**. This lane now matches that speed at under a third of the memory, which was the goal in #34.

New public API: `dgrad_4bit_grouped`, `dgrad_eligible`, `_DGRAD_DEFAULT`, and the `dgrad_kernel` flag on `FusedGroupedNf4` / `gemm_4bit_grouped_train` / `fused_grouped_lora`. Additive only — the default backward is unchanged and still bit-exact.

The CHANGELOG carries the unmeasured-risk note: layer-composed fidelity of the dgrad path has not been measured, and this repo has seen a per-op-more-accurate path cost +0.023% perplexity through 16 layers.

**Publishing**: this repo's `publish.yml` fires on `release: published`, not on tag push — so merging this does not publish. A GitHub Release for `v0.7.0` has to be created after merge.

items.title: readme: refresh performance and memory tables
items.body: Re-measures the README benchmark tables with the documented method unchanged, so rows stay comparable: corpus regenerated from the repo's own sources (same scheme and sizes; the base grew 694 → 706 KB with recent code), speed at a matched `--i15` for both binaries (min of 2, interleaved, idle i9-8950HK), stock rebuilt from a fresh upstream shallow clone, memory as peak RSS via `/usr/bin/time -l` at `--i200` on the 3 MB inputs. ## What changed - **Matched `--i15` speedup**: text ~1.9× → **~2.1×**, incompressible ~2.5–3.5× → **~3.7–4.1×**. - **Peak RSS (3 MB, `--i200`)**: text 22.4 vs 12.3 MB (**−45%**, was −34%); binary 121.3 vs 46.5 MB (**−62%**, was −38%). - Iterations table regenerated on the new base (compressed sizes shift a few bytes with the input drift; both columns of every table were measured on identical bytes, so all in-table comparisons hold). Relative runtimes now ~5.5× at `--i200` / ~25× at `--i1000`, reflecting the cheaper high-iteration passes. - Headline bullets, memory-mechanism list, and prose examples updated to match. ## Confidence Stock's timings reproduce its previous table values almost exactly (e.g. 8.07 s vs 8.13 s on 3 MB text), validating the setup — the deltas are all on the fork side and agree with the independently measured gains from the perf/memory PRs (#11/#12). The fork's memory numbers match the #12 measurements on different random data (12.3/46.5 vs 12.3/45.6 MB). 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) --- Need help on this PR? items.title: Pre-launch number audit: two wrong numbers, one restored section
items.body:
## What this PR does

A full pre-launch pass: every quantitative claim in the README and docs re-measured against a fresh run of the actual benchmark scripts, rather than trusted from memory.

**Two numbers were wrong:**

- *"Our benchmark shows graph memory preserves +5% more information than a summary baseline"* — the real, currently-measured delta is **+10 points** (89% vs 79%), matching every other mention of this same benchmark. The +5% was never updated after the underlying number moved.
- A resume block averaging **"249 tokens"**, cited in two places as *"measured, n=3"* — re-running `benchmarks/checkpoint_accuracy/runner_v2.py` today gives **178 tokens** (197 / 193 / 144 across the three sessions). A third, unrelated "247 tokens" attached to a *fictional* worked example in `docs/architecture.md` was measured against nothing — removed rather than replaced with another fake-precise number.

**Also fixed:**
- `docs/api.md` carried the MCP registry's `mcp-name:` ownership marker as bare visible text instead of an HTML comment — rendered as a stray, out-of-place line in the middle of the MCP setup instructions. New guard test.
- `TESTING.md` described a "no network access" audit environment from an early debugging session that no longer exists, and claimed 23 stdlib tests where the script now runs 25. Rewritten to describe the current suite (600 tests) instead of a frozen historical snapshot.
- `CONTRIBUTING.md`'s project-structure tree said "42 files" for `tests/`; actual count is 44.

items.title: Enhance session management and adaptation features in version 0.2.0

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

items.body:
This pull request introduces a significant new feature: HirayaCoder now learns from actual outcomes to adapt its prompts, improving the user experience without compromising security or permissions. The extension records evidence of what happened during sessions and uses this data to provide corrective hints to the model, helping it avoid repeated mistakes. Several bug fixes related to session management and memory handling are also included.

**Learning and Adaptation:**

* Introduced an outcome ledger (`core/outcomeLedger.js`) that records session and action outcomes locally in `.hirayacoder/outcomes.jsonl`, tracking events like guard refusals, stop reasons, and whether changes were made—without ever recording file paths, commands, or code. This enables the extension to learn from what actually happens in each workspace. [[1]](diffhunk://#diff-06572a96a58dc510037d5efa622f9bec8519bc1beab13c9f251e97e657a9d4edL8-R115) [[2]](diffhunk://#diff-106fd5f9465cadc3b61cafe52252a658d95ba112574c11de91dbecc8f57ed26cR309-R310) [[3]](diffhunk://#diff-106fd5f9465cadc3b61cafe52252a658d95ba112574c11de91dbecc8f57ed26cR333-R341)
* Added earned corrective hints (`agent/earnedHints.js`): when a model trips the same guard three times in a workspace, a corresponding correction is automatically added to its prompt preamble for future sessions, helping the model avoid repeated errors. [[1]](diffhunk://#diff-06572a96a58dc510037d5efa622f9bec8519bc1beab13c9f251e97e657a9d4edL8-R115) [[2]](diffhunk://#diff-106fd5f9465cadc3b61cafe52252a658d95ba112574c11de91dbecc8f57ed26cR375) [[3]](diffhunk://#diff-106fd5f9465cadc3b61cafe52252a658d95ba112574c11de91dbecc8f57ed26cR639-R746)

**Security and Privacy:**

* Ensured that adaptation never weakens guards or permissions and that no sensitive data is recorded in the ledger. Adaptation is strictly limited to what the model is told, not what it is allowed to do.

**Session and Memory Management Fixes:**

* Fixed bugs where new sessions could reuse session numbers, chat tabs could write notes into the wrong session's memory, and clearing session memory did not affect open tabs. Now, session numbers are managed correctly, memory is isolated per session, and clearing memory works as expected.
* Fixed issues where "Show Session Memory" and editor actions could target the wrong session, ensuring actions now follow the last focused tab.

**Other Improvements:**

* Refactored JSONL logging for append-only, robust outcome and audit logging, consolidating logic and ensuring reliability.
* Updated documentation and README to describe the new learning and adaptation features, including commands for inspecting and resetting learned adaptation. [[1]](diffhunk://#diff-06572a96a58dc510037d5efa622f9bec8519bc1beab13c9f251e97e657a9d4edL8-R115) [[2]](diffhunk://#diff-b335630551682c19a781afebcf4d07bf978fb1f8ac04c6bf87428ed5106870f5R20)

These changes collectively make HirayaCoder more helpful and robust, while maintaining strong privacy and security guarantees.

items.title: docs: refresh benchmarks for v0.3.10; move RSS to docs; link Nextflow
items.body:
## What

- **Refresh decode-speed benchmarks** in the README with the v0.3.10 run (sra-tools 3.4.1, 8 CPUs). Speedups vs `fasterq-dump`: 13.1x small / 5.5x medium / 5.4x large; feature line updated to 5-13x.

The page explains the tradeoff: sracha memory-maps column data for zero-copy decode, so its reported peak RSS grows with archive size, whereas `fasterq-dump` uses bounded `pread` and stays flat. Most of the large-file figure is clean, reclaimable page-cache — the real heap working set is ~1.4 GiB — so it's never an OOM risk.
- **Link Nextflow from the README** instead of inlining it. The `groovy` snippet now lives under a `### Nextflow` anchor in the docs; the README points to it, keeping workflow-integration detail off the front page.

## Why

The RSS numbers looked alarming without context (8.4x fasterq-dump on the large fixture) and don't belong on the front page; a docs section can carry the nuance. Investigated the gap by splitting RSS into heap vs file-backed mmap (`smaps_rollup`) and reading ncbi-vdb's read path (`KColumnDataRead` -> `KFileRead`) — the flat fasterq-dump profile is structural (it never mmaps the big columns), not clever page reclaim.

## Notes

- Docs-only; no code changes. `zensical build` passes cleanly.
- `MADV_SEQUENTIAL` was prototyped and dropped (neutral; ~9% on large only) — mmap zero-copy is the deliberate speed tradeoff.

items.title: docs: update annotate runtime/memory figures from benchmark job 35247555
items.body:
Replaces the pre-HKS-era runtime and memory figures in the README and \`docs/commands/annotate.md\` with numbers from a dedicated benchmark (SLURM job 35247555): CHM13v2.0, HG002 v1.1 hap1, and HG002 v1.1 combined diploid, each × {HKS, KMC} × n=3, sequential in one job at \`-t 16\` on an Ice Lake 2.80 GHz node (the machine already described in the README's System requirements). Medians of three; all 18 runs exit 0.

| input | backend | median wall | peak RSS |
|---|---|---|---|
| CHM13 v2.0 | HKS | 8:40 | 10.6 GB |
| CHM13 v2.0 | KMC | 13:19 | 36.1 GB |
| HG002 hap1 | HKS | 7:27 | 10.6 GB |
| HG002 hap1 | KMC | 13:43 | 36.5 GB |
| HG002 diploid | HKS | 15:13 | 10.7 GB |
| HG002 diploid | KMC | 24:22 | 45.9 GB |

What changes and why:

- **KMC runtime, ~17–22 min → ~13–14 min (haplotype).** The old figure traced to the paper's Table S1 serial-sum arithmetic measured on older code and a different machine; today's code (post perf rewrites) measures 13–14 min under the exact scope the README states (one sequential run, assignment plus smoothing for all six sets).
- **annotate.md's "HG002 runs in ~20–30 min"** predated the HKS backend and matched neither backend. Now attributed per backend: HG002 v1.1 combined runs in ~14–16 min (HKS) / ~23–27 min (KMC).
- **HKS claims confirmed, not changed:** ~7–9 min haplotype at a ~10 GB peak, and "a combined diploid is roughly twice that" now carries the measured ~14–16 min.
- **Speedup claim 2.5–3× → 1.5–1.8×** (KMC got faster; HKS RAM is still under a third of KMC's).
- **KMC memory guidance "request ≥ 50 GB" replaced.** The query alone peaks at ~36 GB (haplotype) / ~46 GB (diploid), and the smoothing worker pool that follows counts toward the same allocation under cgroup accounting — the benchmark's first submission at 64 GB was OOM-killed mid-smoothing on a haplotype (job 35247205, watchdog exit 137) while an identical earlier run in the same job squeaked through, so 64 GB is genuinely borderline. Docs now say: request 128 GB (what the benchmark verified) or reduce \`--threads\`, and note that an OOM-killed run resumes past the query step.

Code is untouched — the two \`50 GB\` mentions in \`annotate.py\` are a historical comment and an example in the watchdog's failure message, both still accurate as written.

items.title: fix: migration 006 repairs DBs stranded at v5 with an empty claims table
items.body:
## What changed

Migration 005 shipped in two forms: an early one that created `memory_claims`
empty, and the released one that also backfills it. `migrate()` selects pending
work with `current < target`, so **a DB already stamped v5 by the earlier form
can never run 005 again** - it keeps an empty claims table permanently, and no
reinstall or restart fixes it. Only a new version number reaches it.

Migration 006 re-runs the backfill. It adds no schema.

## Why it is unconditional

Deliberately not guarded on an empty table. A stranded DB that has since stored
one memory containing a ref is no longer empty, and an emptiness guard would
skip it for good. Idempotence instead comes from `INSERT OR IGNORE` against
`UNIQUE (memory_id, kind, ref)`:

- already-populated DB -> a few hundred ms of no-ops, once
- existing `resolved_*` state is preserved (nothing is deleted)
- claims are re-derived from each memory's **current** text, so a ref edited out
  of a memory is not resurrected

## Blast radius

Only DBs upgraded by a pre-release build. PyPI 0.10.0 shipped *with* the
backfill, so every real v4 -> v5 upgrade populated correctly.

## Verification

Rehearsed against a copy of an affected 777-memory database:

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `user_version` | 5 | 6 |
| claim rows | 0 | 151 |

`open 30 / resolved 121 / contradicted 12`, in 190ms. Re-running `migrate()`
afterwards: 0.0ms, no duplicates, memory count intact. Those numbers match the
30 / 118 / 12 predicted from copies before the 0.10.0 release.

## Tests

**371 pass** (367 + 4 new), `ruff` + `black` clean. New cases in
`tests/test_migrations.py`:

- repairs a DB stranded at v5 with an empty claims table
- repairs a stranded DB that is **no longer empty** (why the guard is absent)
- preserves existing resolution state
- does not resurrect a ref edited out of a memory

Existing schema-version assertions bumped 5 -> 6.

## .ai/ knowledge base

| File | Update |
|---|---|
| `.ai/plans/status.md` | Migration 006 entry: root cause, blast radius, rehearsal numbers |
| `.ai/memory.md` | Schema version 5 -> 6 |
| `.ai/specs/01-architecture.md` | Migration 006 noted beside 005 |
| `.ai/specs/dataflow.md` | Exactly-once cuts both ways - an in-place fix reaches only DBs that have not passed the migration |
| `.ai/standards/02-database.md` | **New section:** a shipped migration can never be fixed in place; repairs need a new version number, must be idempotent and unconditional; never point in-development schema code at a live DB |
| `CHANGELOG.md` | `[0.10.1]` entry |

Not updated, with reason: `.ai/specs/product-spec.md` and `README.md` - the tool
surface, setup, configuration, and feature status are all unchanged; this
repairs a migration path only. `.ai/agents/` - no tech stack, directory, or
agent rule changed; `backend.md` already points at `02-database.md`.

## Known debt, not addressed here

`database.py` is now 407 lines, over the 300-line limit (it was 382 before this
change). Pre-existing, same shape as the `storage.py` split nobody has scoped.
Deliberately not bundled into a migration fix.

- Provide a memory-bounded, dependency-free implementation of the numerical MAMA analysis to reduce native memory usage when processing large numbers of SNPs. 
- Preserve the original inverse-based estimator and QC logic from the Python reference while avoiding allocation of M x P x P x P intermediates. 
- Expose the implementation to R users via a small installable package and documented R API for reproducible analysis and replaying fitted coefficients.

### Description

- Add `r-mama/` R package with `DESCRIPTION`, `NAMESPACE`, R wrappers (`R/mama_core.R`) and a detailed `r-mama/README.md` documenting function flow, usage, and numerical behaviour. 
- Implement the numerical core in Rust under `r-mama/src/rust/` with `Cargo.toml` and `lib.rs` providing allocation-bounded matrix construction, QC (`qc_omega`, `tweak_omega`), regression fitting, and the original MAMA estimator logic. 
- Provide a C entrypoint (`r-mama/src/entrypoint.c`) exposing `C_mamars_core`, `C_mamars_analysis`, and `C_mamars_fit` for R via `.Call`, plus `Makevars` to build the Rust static library and link it into the R package. 
- Update top-level `README.md` to advertise the new R / Rust implementation and link into the `r-mama/` docs.

### Testing

- Built the Rust library with `cargo build --release` in `r-mama/src/rust` successfully, producing the static library used by the R package. 
- Ran the Rust unit tests with `cargo test` in `r-mama/src/rust`, and all tests passed.

A complete Connect IQ (Monkey C) watch face project under `triphase/`, implementing the TriPhase build spec v1.0: a data-dense face with 11 metrics permanently on screen, where a time-of-day **emphasis engine** lights 3–4 fields (morning / day / evening phases with user-configurable, midnight-wrapping boundaries, plus a `flat` mode) and dims the rest.

items.title: feat: machine-readable OAuth compatibility list
items.body:
Vendors publish their Basic auth advisories one at a time, as prose, PDFs and
support pages. There is no single place to check whether the thing on your
network has a way out. This is an attempt at one.

`data/devices.json` holds fourteen entries; `docs/DEVICE-COMPATIBILITY.md`
renders them.

## Why structured rather than another table

A JSON file can be read by a script. The audit script could eventually flag
"the mailbox is exposed *and* the device behind it is on the ruled-out list",
which is a decision rather than a report.

The wider reason is links. This project cannot ask anyone for backlinks
without it reading as spam, and it will not rank for the generic queries
before December. What it can do is be the list somebody cites when answering
a forum question about an ineo 266 — because no such list exists.

## Enforced rather than encouraged

**Every entry needs an evidence URL.** The build refuses one without it: a
compatibility list is only worth citing if each row can be checked, and that
property survives only if it cannot be skipped.

The table is generated, and CI runs `--check`. That job is deliberately *not*
gated on the `changes` job — hand-editing the generated page touches no code
file, so a gate on `code == 'true'` would skip precisely the case worth
catching. Verified all three failure modes locally: drift, missing evidence,
unknown status value.

## On accuracy

Only what the advisories document is encoded. No model numbers from memory.

Where a vendor publishes a long, revised per-model list (Ricoh), the entry
says `check-advisory` rather than reproducing numbers that would go stale and
be wrong in someone's hands. Where no public per-model statement was found
(Kyocera), the entry says that rather than implying one exists.

Konica Minolta's is the entry that matters: those ineo models are marked
"N/A" in the vendor's own OAuth column, and the advisory points their owners
at a different mail service instead of an update.

## Also

`docs/ERROR-MESSAGES.md` and `docs/NO-OAUTH-FIRMWARE.md` from the previous two
PRs are cross-linked, and both READMEs and the docs index point at the list.

items.title: Refactor Excel limits handling, validation, and memory management
items.body:
This pull request updates the benchmark results and performance commentary in the `README.md` to reflect the latest measurements and improvements to the ExcelReader library. The changes include updated .NET/runtime versions, revised benchmark numbers, and improved explanations of performance characteristics and tradeoffs, especially for high-cardinality string workloads. The summary and comparison text have also been clarified to better reflect the current state of the library and its competitors.

The most important changes are:

**Benchmark Updates and Results:**
* All benchmark tables and summary statistics have been updated with new timings, memory allocations, and relative performance numbers for ExcelReader and competitor libraries (MiniExcel, Sylvan, SpreadCheetah, Sep, CsvHelper) across XLSX, XLSB, XLS, and CSV formats. This includes both synthetic and real-data workloads, as well as materialized (matched-work) and zero-copy read paths.
* The .NET runtime and SDK versions used for benchmarks have been updated to .NET 10.0.10 (SDK 10.0.302), and references to machine differences and caveats for cross-table comparisons have been removed now that all results are from the same hardware.

**Performance Commentary and Analysis:**
* Commentary has been revised to reflect the new results, including updated speedup and allocation ratios versus competitors, and more accurate descriptions of where ExcelReader leads or matches alternatives.
* The analysis of high-cardinality shared string workloads has been updated: after a fix to the per-reader shared-string deduplication cache (now a pre-sized `string?[]`), ExcelReader allocates less than Sylvan in string-heavy scenarios, where previously it allocated more. This is now explicitly explained in the text.

**Feature and Methodology Clarifications:**
* The explanations for in-memory versus stream-based benchmarks have been clarified, and the results for these paths are now presented from the same benchmark runs.
* The explanation of the `ref struct` parsing path has been updated to reflect the new performance delta (now ~8% faster than the `class` baseline, not 16%).

**Prefetch Decompression Results:**
* The impact of `PrefetchDecompression` is now shown with updated timings and allocation effects, and the commentary on when to use this feature has been slightly revised.

items.title: docs: refresh benchmark numbers (re-run research)
items.body:
Re-ran the footprint benchmark and updated every surface with the current numbers.

## The correction that prompted this

The old table claimed the wasm engine **"reclaims to ~350 MB under load"**. That was a one-off low reading — re-runs are tight and show wasm does **not** shrink; it sits in PGlite's WASM-heap band of **~575–650 MB** (GC-timing dependent). We now present it as a band, not a point value. Confirmed the extensions we eagerly load cost **~0 MB** (bare PGlite measured *higher* than with all 7 loaded), so the wasm figure is inherent to PGlite, not our features.

| binary | native | wasm | PocketBase | Supabase |
|--|--|--|--|--|
| 66 MB | 100 MB | ~640 MB | 24 MB | 1,626 MB |

native/binary grew ~5 MB vs the old table — the real, small cost of the extra bootstrap the recent features added (auth tables, pgmq, cron). PocketBase and Supabase unchanged.

- README footprint table + `assets/footprint.svg` (regenerated, now includes the native engine) + all inline RAM figures

items.title: Phase 06: Implement single-owner task creation (service, draft, UI, tests)
items.body:
### Motivation

- Provide a complete Phase 06 task-creation workflow with a clear mutation boundary that keeps presentation code from mutating DemoDataStore and respects authorization policies. 
- Support deterministic in-memory task IDs/numbers, private drafts, template application, review/confirmation, local audit and sync state, and immediate query refresh so newly created tasks appear in lists.
- Enforce Phase 06 constraints: single-owner assignment only, employee self-task protection, manager/senior-management assignment where authorized, and no backend/Drift/SQLite/cloud features.

### Description

- Added a Flutter-independent command port `TaskCreationService` and a repository-backed implementation `RepositoryTaskCreationService` that composes existing repository and authorization ports and an `AppClock`. 
- Introduced immutable command/value objects: `TaskDraft`, `TaskCreationDefaults`, `TaskCreationOptions`, `TaskValidationResult`, and typed `TaskCreationResult` status and issues, plus `TaskIdentityService` with a deterministic `InMemoryTaskIdentityService`. 
- Implemented centralized validation and business rules enforcing title requirements, category/priority/confidentiality, employee self-ownership, manager assignment checks via `AuthorizationService`, date/effort rules, draft rules, duplicate-submission protection, audit events, and queued local sync operations. 
- Added Riverpod creation providers and `TaskCreationController` that own one authoritative draft, load defaults/options, handle save/submit/delete, invalidate query providers, and reset on logout/profile switch. 
- UI: added a responsive four-step creation flow (Basic, Classification & Planning, Assignment, Review & Submit), template apply/overwrite confirmation, submission confirmation dialog, and a success page; routes added for creation/draft/edit/success and router protection requiring explicit create permissions. 
- Persistence: first draft save assigns stable deterministic id/number and inserts a `Task` record (status = draft); submit updates the task (status = assigned), creates a single `TaskAssignment`, appends an audit event, and enqueues a pending `SyncOperation`. 
- Localization: added matching Arabic and English ARB keys for all new UI strings. 
- Tests and docs: added deterministic unit tests for the creation service and identity service, and updated ARCHITECTURE/DECISIONS/DATA_MODEL/TESTING/IMPLEMENTATION_PROGRESS/README/TASK_CREATION documentation to describe architecture, rules, and limitations. 

### Testing

- Executed automated repository/static checks: ARB JSON parse and Arabic/English key parity check (passed), `git diff --check` (no issues), and a small static delimiter/balance script across Dart files (passed). 
- Unit/widget/provider/router/integration test commands (`flutter test`, `flutter analyze`, `dart format`, `flutter gen-l10n`, `flutter build`, `flutter run`) were not executed because the Flutter/Dart SDK executables are not available in this execution environment; as a result the added Dart tests were created but not run here.

items.title: docs: refresh vs-Blazor baselines; key virtualized rows so Rask wins every scenario
items.body:
## Summary

Refreshes the Rask-vs-Blazor baselines to current code and closes the one scenario where Blazor still won on the wire.

- **`VirtualizationScroll` — key the rows.** The scenario's virtualized rows were unkeyed, so a one-row scroll re-emitted an id+text change for every slot in the window (440 B, a 0.44× *loss* to Blazor's 193 B). Keying rows by item index — the pattern the shipped `VirtualizeItemsDemo` sample already uses, and best practice for any virtualized list — makes a one-row scroll reconcile to a single keyed remove+insert (**52 B, 3.71× win**). Rask now ships fewer wire bytes than Blazor on **all 26 scenarios**.
- **`vs-blazor.md` headline table** refreshed to current `payload-bytes` numbers.
- **Memory footprint section made honest and current.** Per-update allocation *flipped*: it used to be a Blazor win (~69.6 KB vs ~31.5 KB) because the session re-serialised the whole page to a string each update; after the lazy-attribute-path (#284) and reused-char-buffer (#285) changes it is **1,072 B vs Blazor's 42,972 B — Rask wins ~40×**. The one remaining honest Blazor win is **retained heap per mounted tree** (Rask's `Component` object graph vs Blazor's dense frame structs, 0.38–0.59×); the doc now calls that out plainly as the architectural tradeoff.
- **README** gains a fair one-paragraph highlight: wire-byte + per-update-allocation wins, with an explicit pointer to where Blazor wins.

## Testing

- `dotnet build benchmarks/Rask.Benchmarks.VsBlazor -warnaserror` clean; `dotnet format` clean.
- `payload-bytes` confirms 26/26 Rask wins; `mem-footprint` numbers quoted above are from a fresh run on this branch.

items.title: perf: cache infrastructure + throughput profiling for MassSpecGym harness (opt-in, disabled by default)
items.body:
## Summary — updated after review

**Status: addresses all blockers from the first review round. Cache infrastructure now ships
disabled by default (both `--fingerprint-cache-size` and `--inchikey-cache-size` default to `0`),
per the reviewer's own stated fallback criteria, since real-DataLoader-worker peak-RSS+hit-rate
validation was not achieved at any nonzero size.** This PR is profiling results + opt-in,
measured-but-unvalidated-at-scale cache infrastructure — not a claimed fix. The real 50-epoch run
has not been relaunched and won't be until further validation (see README.md's "Not yet done").

### What held up from the first round

- Root cause diagnosis: `RetrievalDataset.__getitem__` re-computing an RDKit InChIKey (label
  matching) and Morgan fingerprint for every candidate on every access, no caching upstream, ~98%
  of `__getitem__`'s wall time — confirmed by `cProfile`, unchanged.
- The InChIKey pass being *larger* than the fingerprint pass (11.5s vs 6.2s over the same sample)
  — unchanged, still a real finding the original "RDKit fingerprinting" framing missed.

### What was wrong, and what changed

1. **The 73x/8-9h projection was a best-case number, correctly called out on review.** A 3-batch
   controlled sample that fit entirely in the cache isn't representative of a real epoch against
   **5,711,803 distinct train candidate SMILES** under an admission-order (not LRU) cache. Built
   an RDKit-free access-pattern simulation (real train fold, real shuffle order, the actual
   admission policy) to get real numbers:

   | cache size | ~memory/worker (packed) | hit rate, epoch 1 | hit rate, epoch 2 |
   |---|---|---|---|
   | 200,000 | ~146MB | ~17.6% | ~18.0% |
   | 1,000,000 | ~730MB | ~53.0% | ~55.0% |
   | 2,000,000 | ~1.46GB | ~70.6% | ~74.7% |
   | 6,000,000 (covers all distinct) | ~4.4GB | ~88.4% | **~100%** |

   Even the "safe-looking" original 200k default only reaches ~18% hit rate at real scale.

2. **Real bug: negative `--fingerprint-cache-size` silently became *unbounded* caching**
   (`x if x > 0 else None`). Fixed with a `cache_size` argparse type that hard-errors on negative
   input (exit code 2, before any of `main()`'s body runs).

3. **The InChIKey cache was unbounded** (`maxsize=None`) — real OOM risk at 5.7M+ entries. New
   `--inchikey-cache-size` flag, same bounded admission policy as fingerprints.

4. **Bit-packed fingerprint storage** (`np.packbits`/`np.unpackbits`): ~731 bytes/entry measured,
   down from ~16KB/entry raw int32. Verified exact round-trip against real `MolFingerprinter`
   output (both miss and hit paths), dtype preserved, and confirmed the downstream
   `torch.as_tensor(..., dtype=X)` conversion is identical regardless of whether the source went
   through the packed cache.

5. **`cache_info()` stats** (hits/misses/admitted/rejected_after_full/current_size/maxsize),
   printed at the end of a `num_workers=0` run (and recorded in `manifest.json`).

6. **`tasks/todo.md` reference removed from public code** — that file is local-only and must not
   be linked from committed code; replaced with a `README.md` pointer.

7. **Found and fixed a real crash**: a literal `%` in an argparse `help=` string collided with
   argparse's own `%`-substitution — `--help` crashed with `TypeError: %i format: a real number is
   required, not dict` until fixed.

8. **`smoke_test.py` gains**: negative-maxsize rejection, `maxsize=0` disabled-cache parity
   (identical output to the unwrapped transform), a serialization round-trip test (moved the
   test's own counting-transform helper to module level after hitting the *exact*
   function-local-class pickling bug this whole PR is about — same class of bug
   `_RetrievalDatasetWithCandidates` already documents), and a packed-fingerprint round-trip check
   (numpy-conditional, so the script still runs with neither massspecgym nor numpy installed).

### Real-worker measurement — attempted, only partially completed

Intended scope: shuffle=True, `--num-workers 1` (current default), 100–300 batches, no-cache vs.
cache, throughput + hit rate + peak RSS. **Only the no-cache half completed in practical time** —
15 train + 5 val batches alone took ~10 minutes wall-clock, making 100–300 batches (let alone a
full ~3,033-batch epoch) impractical within this investigation.

What it did surface, and it's real: **`--num-workers 1` measured 40.3s/batch — slower than
`--num-workers 0`'s 12.48s/batch**, not faster. A single worker adds pickling/IPC overhead for
large per-item tensors without providing parallelism to offset it. Not investigated further, not
acted on (didn't change the default), but flagged in `README.md` as worth checking before any real
relaunch — the current default may not even be a good choice here, independent of caching.

Peak-RSS instrumentation in that same run produced an **internally inconsistent, untrustworthy
number** (a `psutil`-based "peak combined RSS" only 29MB above baseline, while direct `ps`-table
inspection mid-run showed a single worker process at ~856MB RSS on its own) — a real bug in the
measurement script that wasn't tracked down given time already spent. This is called out
explicitly as unreliable in `README.md`, not presented as a valid result.

## Merge-readiness, per the reviewer's own criteria

> 次のどちらかならPR #14をマージできます：(1) packed fingerprint＋bounded InChIKey cacheで、
> worker込みのpeak RSSとhit rateが妥当 (2) キャッシュをdefault disabledにし、今回のPRを
> 「profiling結果＋opt-in cache infrastructure」として正確に位置付ける

Going with **(2)**: real-worker peak-RSS+hit-rate validation wasn't achieved (see above), so both
cache flags default to `0`/disabled. Enabling either is a deliberate opt-in with the measured
hit-rate/memory table as a starting point, not a recommendation.

## Test plan

- `python3 smoke_test.py` — all checks (6, 6b–6f) pass, run both with and without the massspecgym
  venv activated.
- `python3 run_baseline.py --help` — exits 0 (previously crashed on the `%`-formatting bug).
- `python3 run_baseline.py --fingerprint-cache-size -1 --out-dir /tmp/x` / same for
  `--inchikey-cache-size` — both exit 2 with a clear error message.
- Packed-cache round-trip verified against real `MolFingerprinter` output (not just synthetic
  data), including the downstream `torch.as_tensor` dtype-conversion check.
- Access-pattern simulation numbers cross-checked against `tracemalloc`-measured real per-entry
  memory costs (fingerprint ~731B, InChIKey ~107B).
- No `masstrust-core`/`masstrust-cli`/Rust changes — Rust CI matrix unaffected.

items.title: feat(service): Transport reader seam — stream SERVICE body without String buffering (sq-my8wd.5)
items.body:
> 🤖 SPARQ agent — `sq-my8wd.5` SERVICE federation memory optimisation (sub-epic sq-my8wd, part of sq-6tykl)

## Summary

- Introduces `ReaderTransport` trait and `TransportAsReader` adapter in `sparq-engine-service` so the SPARQL-results parser consumes the HTTP response body as a streaming `Read`, never as a full `String`.
- `eval_remote_into_read` (new public fn) replaces `eval_remote_into` on the hot path in `exec.rs`; `HttpTransport` implements `ReaderTransport` via ureq's `into_body().into_with_config().limit(N).reader()` — no `read_to_string`.
- The existing `Transport` interface (and all test doubles that implement it) is unchanged; `TransportAsReader` wraps any `Transport` as a `ReaderTransport` via `Cursor<String>` so test mocks continue working without modification.
- `parse_results_into_read` content-sniffs the first non-whitespace byte on a `BufRead` and dispatches to `parse_srj_into_read` (serde_json `Deserializer::from_reader`) or `parse_srx_into_read` (quick_xml `Reader::from_reader`).
- Result semantics are preserved exactly: same solutions, same order, same error propagation on truncated/malformed responses — the streaming reader parsers are verified against the existing string-based implementations in the `streaming_equivalence` suite.
- Feature remains behind the existing off-by-default `service` cargo feature; `sparq-core`/`sparq-engine` default builds are unaffected.

## Load-bearing invariant

`transport_reader_seam_peak_stays_below_body_size` — a thread-local byte-counting allocator asserts peak allocation during `eval_remote_into_read` on a 10 000-row SRJ body stays below `body_len + 4 MiB`. This is the acceptance test for the buffering elimination. All 15 federation integration tests (incl. the existing `large_service_result_consumption_is_bounded_by_the_body_not_the_relation`) remain green.

## Gates run (both feature states)

| Gate | Default (feature OFF) | With `--features service` |
|---|---|---|
| `cargo build` | green | green |
| `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` | green | green |
| `cargo test` | green | green (69 unit + 15 federation) |
| `RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings" cargo doc --workspace --no-deps --all-features` | green | n/a (same run) |
| `python3 scripts/check-readme-template.py --enforce` | 0 deviations (52 READMEs) | — |

## Perf note

Peak memory measurement numbers are work-box timings (non-canonical EC2 dev box) — see AGENTS.md. The absolute values are not documented; only the bounded invariant (peak < body_len + 4 MiB) is asserted in the test.

## Files changed

- `crates/sparq-engine-service/src/service.rs` — `ReaderTransport`, `TransportAsReader`, `eval_remote_into_read`, `parse_results_into_read`, `parse_srj_into_read`, `parse_srx_into_read`, `impl ReaderTransport for HttpTransport`; 5 direct unit tests added for coverage ratchet
- `crates/sparq-engine/src/exec.rs` — `service_reader_transport` module (delegates to `service_transport::with_opt`); `eval_service` + `bound_join_service_single` updated to use reader path
- `crates/sparq-engine/tests/federation_features/service_stream_bounded.rs` — `transport_reader_seam_peak_stays_below_body_size` test (the load-bearing acceptance invariant)
- `crates/sparq-engine-service/README.md` — documents the reader seam and its memory bound

Closes sq-my8wd.5 · sub-epic sq-my8wd · parent epic sq-6tykl

items.title: docs: refresh DOOP FlowLog-vs-Souffle benchmark on main-next (20/20, geomean 3.52x)
items.body:
## What

Refresh the **DOOP `default` points-to** FlowLog-vs-Soufflé benchmark in the README
("vs Soufflé — DOOP") with a fresh run on **current `main-next` (`70c99a8`)**, and add
the peak-memory chart alongside the run-time chart.

- Updates `docs/doop-time.png`, adds `docs/doop-memory.png`
- Refreshes the README numbers (intro summary + the DOOP section)

## Method

`doop/default.dl` across **all 20 DaCapo 23.11-MR2-chopin apps** at **32 threads** —
FlowLog `-w 32` vs Soufflé 2.5 `-j 32`. The Soufflé program is the *same* `default.dl`
with only type-keyword renames (`:string`→`:symbol`, `:int32`→`:number`) — **identical
rules and written join order**. Run only is timed (median of 3; one-off compile
excluded); peak RSS via `/usr/bin/time -v`.

### Both engines truly run on 32 threads
Soufflé is compiled **and** run with `-j 32` — both are required (`souffle -o` without
`-j 32` emits sequential code that ignores the runtime `-j`). Verified this run:

- **Compile-side:** all 20 Soufflé binaries link `libgomp` (parallel-ready).
- **Run-side (`/usr/bin/time -v` CPU%):** Soufflé **642–1501%**, FlowLog **2871–3196%** —
  i.e. genuinely multi-core on both sides. Sanity check on `batik`: same binary is
  **112.6 s @ 99% CPU** at `-j 1` vs **28.2 s @ 1215% CPU** at `-j 32`.

So the speedups are a real 32-thread-vs-32-thread comparison, not a single-threaded-Soufflé artifact.

## Results (this run)

- ✅ **Correctness — 20/20 identical `VarPointsTo`** (per-app `.printsize` crosscheck).
- ⚡ **Run time — FlowLog faster on 20/20, geomean `3.62×`** (range `1.41×`–`6.07×`),
  up from the previous `1.95×`. Big engine gains since the last snapshot — e.g.
  **graphchi 1.6×→6.1×**, **h2o 1.7×→5.5×**; jython (438 M `VarPointsTo`) tightest at 1.4×.
- 🧠 **Peak memory — Soufflé/FlowLog geomean `0.43×`** (FlowLog trades memory for speed).

![run time](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/flowlog-rs/flowlog/bench/doop-plot-refresh-main-next/docs/doop-time.png)

items.title: NA/zoned: implement RAP A* heuristic (Eqs. 3-5) so routing-aware search completes (#297)
items.body:
## Summary

Implements [RAP] (Stade, Lin, Cong, Wille, ICCAD 2025, arXiv:2505.22715) Sec. IV-B/IV-C/V-C/V-D — the A* heuristic (Eqs. 3–5) that `assign_aware_legal` (`quon_na/src/zoned.rs`) previously did not have. Before this PR, the routing-aware search was **uniform-cost** (`h = 0`): on the RAP Table I anchor fixture (`test/na/ising_n42.qn`, 82 two-qubit gates / 4 entangling layers, 340 candidate pairs, up to 21 simultaneous gates per layer), it exhausted its 100,000-expansion budget on **every layer**, so routing-aware fell back to greedy every time and produced byte-for-byte identical output to routing-agnostic — this was the "Phase 1 finding" in `docs/neutral_atom/rap_table_i_methodology.md`.

This PR closes that gap: the aware search now completes (finds a full legal assignment) on all 4 layers of the anchor fixture, and genuinely beats routing-agnostic.

**Fixes #297.**

## What changed algorithmically

- **Eq. (1) grouping moved *into* the search.** Before, each search node's cost summed every gate's own `√d_max` independently — it never modeled AOD-compatible movement grouping, so it didn't match what `partition_aod_compatible` actually charges post-search. `assign_aware_legal` now maintains the same grouping (`positions_aod_compatible`) incrementally per node, so `cost_so_far` is exact Eq. (1) cost, not a proxy.
- **Eqs. (3)–(4) heuristic.** Admissible part: `max(0, √(max distance among unplaced gates' nearest still-legal pair) − √(current largest group distance))`. Accelerating part: `δ · (β + Σ_G SD(G)) · |unplaced|`. `SD(G)` is computed on **discrete ranks** of each group's source/target coordinates (matching the paper's own discretization, Sec. V-A/V-C/Example 9), *not* raw µm displacement — an earlier draft used raw displacement directly, and while implementing the scaled-up unit test below I caught it blowing the heuristic up (hundreds of µm-scale "spurious" penalty) whenever one group member's move happened to be physically much longer than another's, even in perfectly legal, uniform-in-the-only-sense-that-matters groups. See the commit / module doc for the full story.
- **Sec. IV-C/IV-B sign resolution.** The paper's printed Eq. (3) reads ambiguously as a bare subtraction; I cross-checked against qmap's actual C++ (`munich-quantum-toolkit/qmap`, `src/na/zoned/layout_synthesizer/placer/HeuristicPlacer.cpp`'s `getHeuristic`/`sumStdDeviationForGroups`, fetched via WebFetch) to confirm it's `max(0, √unplaced − √placed)`, and that δ/β are qmap's `deepeningFactor`/`deepeningValue`.
- **Sec. V-D pruning window.** Bounds each gate's considered candidates per node to the nearest `pruning_window` *legal* pairs — scanned from the full legal set (not truncated before legality filtering), so completeness is preserved.
- **Sec. V-A movement-group compatibility.** Already existed post-search (`partition_aod_compatible`/`moves_aod_compatible`); factored out the shared per-axis check (`positions_aod_compatible`) so the search's in-node grouping and the post-search router use identical legality logic. Linear-scan, not qmap's BST — a documented data-structure simplification (legal at this crate's per-layer sizes), not a legality-semantics one.
- **Beam width — not from the paper.** The single largest lever empirically. Without a frontier cap, the priority queue at `ising_n42` scale (20–21 simultaneous gates, 340 pairs, real crosstalk conflicts between geometrically adjacent entanglement-zone pairs — `min_rydberg_spacing_um = 18.75` vs. pair pitch `(12, 10)` µm) filled with a huge number of shallow (early-gate) alternatives that all looked similarly cheap under the heuristic; I measured the frontier reaching 1M+ queued nodes while still stuck below half depth on a 20–21-gate layer, with 100,000 expansions spent almost entirely widening rather than deepening. Trimming the frontier to the best `beam_width` nodes whenever it exceeds `2 × beam_width` (standard beam search) forces the search to commit to promising partial placements. This is a departure from the paper's (unspecified) search-loop mechanics, not from its legality semantics.

**Not implemented (documented scope reduction, not an oversight):** Eq. (5)'s cross-layer look-ahead term, and Eq. (2)'s `α`/`γ` reuse-cost terms it depends on. This module's search only decides gate→pair assignment *within one layer* (no atom-by-atom intermediate/storage placement across layers — that's a pre-existing scope boundary of `assign_aware_legal`, unrelated to this PR), so there's no "next gate's partner" to look ahead to without a larger restructuring of the search shape.

## Parameters (`AwareSearchParams`, `quon_na/src/zoned.rs`)

| Parameter | Value | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `deepening_factor` (δ) | 0.6 | [RAP] Sec. VI-A QASMBench parameter set — `ising_n42` is itself a QASMBench benchmark (Table I's `ising2` row) |
| `deepening_value` (β) | 0.2 | Same QASMBench set |
| `node_budget` | 100,000 | Unchanged from the old `AWARE_NODE_BUDGET` constant — now genuinely sufficient given the heuristic + beam width, rather than always being exhausted |
| `pruning_window` | 32 | Chosen empirically; qmap's own window size wasn't discoverable from the parts of `HeuristicPlacer` I could fetch |
| `beam_width` | 2,000 | Swept 500 / 1,000 / 2,000 / 3,000 / 4,000 / 5,000 on the real fixture; 2,000 was the smallest value that still gave the best steps/time pair among values completing all 4 layers within budget |

α and γ have no field — see "Not implemented" above.

**Config placement:** `AwareSearchParams` lives on `NaScheduleOptions::aware_search` (per-run option), not the target JSON — this matches qmap's own shape, where the analogous `Config` is passed to the placer per call rather than baked into the architecture description. `schedule_zoned`'s existing 3-arg signature is preserved as a thin wrapper over the new `schedule_zoned_with_aware_params`, so none of its ~11 existing call sites needed to change.

## Verified results

**`ising_n42` / `rap_table_i.json`** (`cargo test --release -p quonc --test rap_table_i -- --include-ignored --nocapture`, real output):

```
placer                  steps    (paper)  time_us(move)        (paper)        transfer_us       aware search
routing-agnostic           23         22           3049           3100               4890                n/a
routing-aware              18          9           2999           1600               4890 4 ok / 0 fell back
```

- `aware_search_fell_back_layers == 0` ✅ (was 4/4 before this PR)
- Routing-aware rearrangement steps (18) strictly below routing-agnostic (23) ✅ — and move-only time (2999 µs) also improved slightly (3049 µs)
- Pre-flight invariants unchanged: 82 `entangle2` gates, 4 Rydberg stages, both placer modes — `ising_n42_preflight_gate_and_layer_counts` and the dump test's structural asserts both pass
- Runtime: ~5s combined for both placers in `--release` (was ~90–125s pre-#297, always hitting budget on every layer)
- **Peak RSS dropped from ~17.5 GB to ~64 MB** on this same fixture (measured via `/usr/bin/time -l`) — a side effect of the search actually completing instead of endlessly growing an unbounded frontier. `justfile`'s `rap-table-i` recipe comment updated to record this; the recipe itself is left local-only (not re-wired into `ci-rust`'s hosted-runner gate) since that's a separate decision out of this PR's scope.
- I did **not** hit the exact published 9-step/1.6ms row — see the new "Divergences from the paper's numbers" section in `docs/neutral_atom/rap_table_i_methodology.md` for the believed reasons (no cross-layer look-ahead, no storage-zone re-optimization, beam-width/budget vs. qmap's presumably much larger default).

**Existing/new unit tests** (`quon_na/src/zoned.rs`):
- `aware_search_completes_and_beats_greedy_on_contended_pairs` (pre-existing, 2-gate/2-pair) — still passes unchanged.
- `aware_search_completes_and_beats_greedy_at_ising_n42_scale` (new) — same contention shape replicated across 10 well-separated clusters (20 gates, 340 candidate pairs total, matching `ising_n42`'s real per-layer scale). This is the test that caught the raw-µm-displacement SD bug during development (it tied with greedy until the rank-based fix landed).

## What I did *not* do

Per the issue's explicit instruction: **I did not set `QUON_RAP_TABLE_I_ENFORCE=1`.** `docs/neutral_atom/rap_table_i_methodology.md`'s Phase 2 is now split into 2a (this PR: land the working heuristic) and 2b (human sign-off, then flip the enforcement flag) — see the new "Phase 2a status" section for the numbers a human should look at before making that call, including the honest gap to the paper's published row.

## Stale-numbers check

Per the task brief, grepped `samples/research/` and `samples/visualization/goldens/` for anything pinned to the old aware-search behavior:
- `samples/research/na_resource_study_smoke.py` / `na_resource_study.ipynb` — only pin `estimated_cycles`/`rearrangement_steps`/`trap_transfers` for `qaoa_graph.qn`, all unaffected by this change (only `total_time_us`, which they don't pin, moved on that fixture). Re-ran the smoke script directly — still passes.
- `quonc/tests/na_showcase.rs`'s `placer_headline_numbers_match_readme` **did** need updating (`qaoa_graph.qn` aware `total_time_us` 1764→1742; `ising.qn` aware now ties agnostic on every metric including `total_time_us`, 2256→2217) — updated the pinned numbers, `samples/neutral-atom/README.md`'s matching table/prose, and replaced the old "N2" non-fallback proof (which relied on `total_time_us` differing, no longer true) with a direct `--emit-na-stats` diagnostic check instead — a strictly more robust proof than the numeric-side-effect one it replaces.
- `samples/visualization/goldens/na_schedule_metrics/*.json` — routing-agnostic only, unaffected.

## Local verification

- `cargo fmt --check` — clean
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` — clean
- `cargo test --workspace` — 152/152 test blocks pass, 0 failures (ran twice, once before and once after rebasing onto the #305 PR that landed on `main` mid-session)
- `cargo test --release -p quonc --test rap_table_i -- --include-ignored --nocapture` — passes, numbers above, reproduced twice
- `quon_na/tests/snapshots/stats_snapshots__zoned_routing_aware*.snap` — regenerated via `INSTA_UPDATE=always` (new `aware_search_deepening_factor`/`_deepening_value`/`_pruning_window` fields on `SearchDiagnostics`, and `node_expansions` moved with the algorithm change)

## Files touched

- `quon_na/src/zoned.rs` — the core algorithm change (`AwareSearchParams`, heuristic, beam trim, grouping-in-search, module doc)
- `quon_na/src/pipeline.rs`, `quon_na/src/qec_schedule.rs` — thread `NaScheduleOptions::aware_search` through
- `quon_na/src/stats.rs` — new `SearchDiagnostics` fields for `--emit-na-stats`
- `quon_na/src/lib.rs`, `quonc/src/compile.rs` — re-exports / config plumbing
- `quon_na/tests/pipeline.rs`, `quon_na/tests/stats_snapshots.rs` + regenerated `.snap` files — mechanical `NaScheduleOptions` field addition + snapshot refresh
- `quonc/tests/na_showcase.rs`, `samples/neutral-atom/README.md` — pinned-number and narrative updates (see "Stale-numbers check")
- `docs/neutral_atom/rap_table_i_methodology.md` — new "Phase 2a status" section, updated runtime/memory numbers, Phase 1 section marked superseded (kept as historical record)
- `Justfile` — updated stale memory-usage comment on the `rap-table-i` recipe

items.title: Docs: Update docs to latest implementations
items.body:
A review of all 17 published docs (README, CONTRIBUTING, docs/, the docs-site home, and the collector runbook) against three tiers of ground truth:

1. the binary's own `--help` output for every documented command and flag,
2. the Go source for every number (ports, thresholds, timeouts, paths),
3. the official Canton / Splice / CIP documentation for upstream claims, plus a liveness probe of every external link.

72 verified errors, all corrected. Highlights by class:

**Commands that fail as written** — README's Homebrew one-liner used a nonexistent tap name; the APT example pinned version 0.7.0 (never published) and the direct-.deb example targeted a release with no .deb asset; `doctor --name`, `ui --name`, positional `logs <service>`, and bare `dar upload` don't exist in the binary.

**Misattributed behavior** — the tokens-v2 profile warning comes from `up`, not `doctor`; `contracts watch` auto-discovers the participant endpoint and JWT from the registry (`--endpoint` is an override, not a requirement).

**Retired formats still documented** — snapshot/restore text described the old docker-volume tarball; the shipped format is a logical `pg_dumpall` plus registry state from a running instance. The same stale wording was in the CLI's `localnet --help` table and the Web UI's Backup & restore subtitle — fixed on all three surfaces.

**Dashboard customization rebuilt around the real contract** — the guide edited the repo's dashboard JSON, which no container mounts; the live path is the per-instance copy under `~/.canton-devkit/localnet/<name>/observability/grafana/`. Also fixed: compose project names (`canton-<name>`), a nonexistent `grafana-data` volume, invented Grafana credentials (access is anonymous), and Grafana 11 alerting behavior.

**Invented CLI transcripts** — the README/docs-home `localnet up` sample printed lines the binary never emits; replaced with the real step headers and welcome summary reconstructed from the progress/welcome source strings.

**Numbers** — readiness timeout 25 min, per-version memory floors (8 GB for the 0.6 line), Docker Desktop defaulting to 50% of host memory, 16 GB public GitHub runners, metric-prefix count matching its own table, resource-limit arithmetic that adds up.

**Readability** — every backticked command with a trailing ellipsis (`dpm localnet …` etc.) now spells the explicit `<command>` form; dead links repointed (`docs.daml.com/canton/` → `docs.canton.network`).

Verification: full Go suite, 214/214 frontend tests, 16-page site build, and an independent review of the applied diff against the findings list (zero missed; one wording regression caught and fixed before commit).

items.title: v1.0.0: Security, Stability & Test Coverage
items.body:
### Security fixes (3 audit reports)

- Email verification now actually updates email_verified in DB (was cosmetic only)
- Login timing attack mitigated: bcrypt always runs (dummy hash for unknown emails)
- Nginx: restored CSP/X-Frame-Options on static files (child location was stripping parent headers)
- Sentry: request body filtered to prevent password/PII leaks
- Goal Seek: max data size validation to prevent DoS (100x50 cells)
- Docker: npm prune --omit=dev to reduce attack surface, native Node.js healthcheck
- Rate limiting: removed in-memory fallback, trust express-rate-limit

### Bug fixes

- Numbers now right-aligned by default (Excel behavior)
- Active-cell highlight clears immediately on new click (no stale green)
- Selection stays visible when clicking ribbon/format buttons
- Course detail page always starts at top
- setDataAtCell with formulas now triggers HF recalculation
- Name box now shows range reference (e.g. A1:B5) on multi-cell selection

### Tests — 198 backend + 81 frontend + 79 E2E

- Backend: +30 tests (middleware auth, email verification, goal-seek validation, pagination, timing attacks, exercise structure)
- Frontend: 5 new suites (Sparkline utils, QuizExercise, DataValidationDialog, GoalSeekDialog, ConditionalFormatDialog)
- E2E: Fixed auth helpers (field names, localStorage key), quiz-aware selectors, spreadsheet-specific exercise finder, page.reload() isolation for formula tests, teacher panel, student panel, course navigation
- All broken tests fixed; flaky formula tests made reliable

### Performance & UX

- Courses N+1 query replaced with single bulk query
- bcrypt.hashSync to async hash in teacher route
- Teacher endpoints: pagination on /students and /analytics
- outsideClickDeselects: false keeps selection visible on focus loss

### Docs & CI

- CI workflow renamed to CI, HTML reporter set to open: never
- playwright-report/ and test-results/ added to .gitignore
- Version bumped to 1.0.0
- README & ARCHITECTURE.md updated (versions, test counts, removed nonexistent PostgreSQL, fixed license)
