5.6.0
=====

:release-date: 2025-11-30
:release-by: Tomer Nosrati

Celery v5.6.0 is now available.

Key Highlights
```

See :ref:`whatsnew-5.6` for a complete overview or read the main highlights below.

## Python 3.9 Minimum Version

Celery 5.6.0 drops support for Python 3.8 (EOL). The minimum required Python
version is now 3.9. Users still on Python 3.8 must upgrade their Python version
before upgrading to Celery 5.6.0.

Additionally, this release includes initial support for Python 3.14.

## SQS: Reverted to `pycurl` from `urllib3`

The switch from `pycurl` to `urllib3` for the SQS transport (introduced in
Celery 5.5.0 via Kombu) has been reverted due to critical issues affecting SQS
users:

- Processing throughput dropped from \~100 tasks/sec to \~3/sec in some environments
- `UnknownOperationException` errors causing container crash loops
- Silent message processing failures with no error logs

Users of the SQS transport must ensure `pycurl` is installed. If you removed
`pycurl` after upgrading to Celery 5.5.0, you will need to reinstall it.

Contributed by `@auvipy <https://github.com/auvipy>`\_ in
`#​9620 <https://github.com/celery/celery/pull/9620>`\_.

## Security Fix: Broker Credential Leak Prevention

Fixed a security issue where broker URLs containing passwords were being logged
in plaintext by the delayed delivery mechanism. Broker credentials are now
properly sanitized in all log output.

Contributed by `@giancarloromeo <https://github.com/giancarloromeo>`\_ in
`#​9997 <https://github.com/celery/celery/pull/9997>`\_.

## Memory Leak Fixes

Two significant memory leaks have been fixed in this release:

**Exception Handling Memory Leak**: Fixed a critical memory leak in task exception
handling that was particularly severe on Python 3.11+ due to enhanced traceback
data. The fix properly breaks reference cycles in tracebacks to allow garbage
collection.

Contributed by `@jaiganeshs21 <https://github.com/jaiganeshs21>`\_ in
`#​9799 <https://github.com/celery/celery/pull/9799>`\_.

**Pending Result Memory Leak**: Fixed a memory leak where `AsyncResult`
subscriptions were not being cleaned up when results were forgotten.

Contributed by `@tsoos99dev <https://github.com/tsoos99dev>`\_ in
`#​9806 <https://github.com/celery/celery/pull/9806>`\_.

## ETA Task Memory Limit

New configuration option :setting:`worker_eta_task_limit` to prevent out-of-memory
crashes when workers fetch large numbers of ETA or countdown tasks. Previously,
workers could exhaust available memory when the broker contained many scheduled tasks.

Example usage:

.. code-block:: python

```
app.conf.worker_eta_task_limit = 1000
```

Contributed by `@sashu2310 <https://github.com/sashu2310>`\_ in
`#​9853 <https://github.com/celery/celery/pull/9853>`\_.

## Queue Type Selection for Auto-created Queues

New configuration options allow specifying the queue type and exchange type when
Celery auto-creates missing queues. This is particularly useful for RabbitMQ users
who want to use quorum queues with auto-created queues.

Configuration options:

- :setting:`task_create_missing_queue_type`: Sets the queue type for auto-created
  queues (e.g., `quorum`, `classic`)
- :setting:`task_create_missing_queue_exchange_type`: Sets the exchange type for
  auto-created queues

Example usage:

.. code-block:: python

```
app.conf.task_create_missing_queue_type = 'quorum'
```

Contributed by `@ghirailghiro <https://github.com/ghirailghiro>`\_ in
`#​9815 <https://github.com/celery/celery/pull/9815>`\_.

Key Highlights

```

See :ref:`whatsnew-5.5` for a complete overview or read the main highlights below.

Redis Broker Stability Improvements
-----------------------------------

Long-standing disconnection issues with the Redis broker have been identified and
resolved in Kombu 5.5.0, which is included with this release. These improvements
significantly enhance stability when using Redis as a broker.

Additionally, the Redis backend now has better exception handling with the new
``exception_safe_to_retry`` feature, which improves resilience during temporary
Redis connection issues. See :ref:`conf-redis-result-backend` for complete
documentation.

Contributed by `@drienkop <https://github.com/drienkop>`_ in
`#​9614 <https://github.com/celery/celery/pull/9614>`_.

``pycurl`` replaced with ``urllib3``
------------------------------------

Replaced the :pypi:`pycurl` dependency with :pypi:`urllib3`.

We're monitoring the performance impact of this change and welcome feedback from users
who notice any significant differences in their environments.

Contributed by `@spawn-guy <https://github.com/spawn-guy>`_ in Kombu
`#​2134 <https://github.com/celery/kombu/pull/2134>`_ and integrated in Celery via
`#​9526 <https://github.com/celery/celery/pull/9526>`_.

RabbitMQ Quorum Queues Support
------------------------------

Added support for RabbitMQ's new `Quorum Queues <https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/quorum-queues>`_
feature, including compatibility with ETA tasks. This implementation has some limitations compared
to classic queues, so please refer to the documentation for details.

`Native Delayed Delivery <https://docs.particular.net/transports/rabbitmq/delayed-delivery>`_
is automatically enabled when quorum queues are detected to implement the ETA mechanism.

See :ref:`using-quorum-queues` for complete documentation.

Configuration options:

- :setting:`broker_native_delayed_delivery_queue_type`: Specifies the queue type for
  delayed delivery (default: ``quorum``)
- :setting:`task_default_queue_type`: Sets the default queue type for tasks
  (default: ``classic``)
- :setting:`worker_detect_quorum_queues`: Controls automatic detection of quorum
  queues (default: ``True``)

Contributed in `#​9207 <https://github.com/celery/celery/pull/9207>`_,
`#​9121 <https://github.com/celery/celery/pull/9121>`_, and
`#​9599 <https://github.com/celery/celery/pull/9599>`_.

For details regarding the 404 errors, see
`New Year's Security Incident <https://github.com/celery/celery/discussions/9525>`_.

Soft Shutdown Mechanism
-----------------------

Soft shutdown is a time limited warm shutdown, initiated just before the cold shutdown.
The worker will allow :setting:`worker_soft_shutdown_timeout` seconds for all currently
executing tasks to finish before it terminates. If the time limit is reached, the worker
will initiate a cold shutdown and cancel all currently executing tasks.

This feature is particularly valuable when using brokers with visibility timeout
mechanisms, such as Redis or SQS. It allows the worker enough time to re-queue
tasks that were not completed before exiting, preventing task loss during worker
shutdown.

See :ref:`worker-stopping` for complete documentation on worker shutdown types.

Configuration options:

- :setting:`worker_soft_shutdown_timeout`: Sets the duration in seconds for the soft
  shutdown period (default: ``0.0``, disabled)
- :setting:`worker_enable_soft_shutdown_on_idle`: Controls whether soft shutdown
  should be enabled even when the worker is idle (default: ``False``)

Contributed by `@Nusnus <https://github.com/Nusnus>`_ in
`#​9213 <https://github.com/celery/celery/pull/9213>`_,
`#​9231 <https://github.com/celery/celery/pull/9231>`_, and
`#​9238 <https://github.com/celery/celery/pull/9238>`_.

Pydantic Support
----------------

New native support for Pydantic models in tasks. This integration
allows you to leverage Pydantic's powerful data validation and serialization
capabilities directly in your Celery tasks.

Example usage:

.. code-block:: python

    from pydantic import BaseModel
    from celery import Celery

    app = Celery('tasks')

    class ArgModel(BaseModel):
        value: int

    class ReturnModel(BaseModel):
        value: str

    @app.task(pydantic=True)
    def x(arg: ArgModel) -> ReturnModel:

### args/kwargs type hinted as Pydantic model will be converted
        assert isinstance(arg, ArgModel)

### The returned model will be converted to a dict automatically
        return ReturnModel(value=f"example: {arg.value}")

See :ref:`task-pydantic` for complete documentation.

Configuration options:

- ``pydantic=True``: Enables Pydantic integration for the task
- ``pydantic_strict=True/False``: Controls whether strict validation is enabled
  (default: ``False``)
- ``pydantic_context={...}``: Provides additional context for validation
- ``pydantic_dump_kwargs={...}``: Customizes serialization behavior

Contributed by `@mathiasertl <https://github.com/mathiasertl>`_ in
`#​9023 <https://github.com/celery/celery/pull/9023>`_,
`#​9319 <https://github.com/celery/celery/pull/9319>`_, and
`#​9393 <https://github.com/celery/celery/pull/9393>`_.

Google Pub/Sub Transport
------------------------

New support for Google Cloud Pub/Sub as a message transport, expanding
Celery's cloud integration options.

See :ref:`broker-gcpubsub` for complete documentation.

For the Google Pub/Sub support you have to install additional dependencies:

.. code-block:: console

    $ pip install "celery[gcpubsub]"

Then configure your Celery application to use the Google Pub/Sub transport:

.. code-block:: python

    broker_url = 'gcpubsub://projects/project-id'

Contributed by `@haimjether <https://github.com/haimjether>`_ in
`#​9351 <https://github.com/celery/celery/pull/9351>`_.

Python 3.13 Support
-------------------

Official support for Python 3.13. All core dependencies have been
updated to ensure compatibility, including Kombu and py-amqp.

This release maintains compatibility with Python 3.8 through 3.13, as well as
PyPy 3.10+.

Contributed by `@Nusnus <https://github.com/Nusnus>`_ in
`#​9309 <https://github.com/celery/celery/pull/9309>`_ and
`#​9350 <https://github.com/celery/celery/pull/9350>`_.

REMAP_SIGTERM Support
---------------------

The "REMAP_SIGTERM" feature, previously undocumented, has been tested, documented,
and is now officially supported. This feature allows you to remap the SIGTERM
signal to SIGQUIT, enabling you to initiate a soft or cold shutdown using TERM
instead of QUIT.

This is particularly useful in containerized environments where SIGTERM is the
standard signal for graceful termination.

See :ref:`Cold Shutdown documentation <worker-REMAP_SIGTERM>` for more info.

To enable this feature, set the environment variable:

.. code-block:: bash

    export REMAP_SIGTERM="SIGQUIT"

Contributed by `@Nusnus <https://github.com/Nusnus>`_ in
`#​9461 <https://github.com/celery/celery/pull/9461>`_.

Database Backend Improvements
-----------------------------

New ``create_tables_at_setup`` option for the database
backend. This option controls when database tables are created, allowing for
non-lazy table creation.

By default (``create_tables_at_setup=True``), tables are created during backend
initialization. Setting this to ``False`` defers table creation until they are
actually needed, which can be useful in certain deployment scenarios where you want
more control over database schema management.

See :ref:`conf-database-result-backend` for complete documentation.

Configuration:

.. code-block:: python

    app.conf.result_backend = 'db+sqlite:///results.db'
    app.conf.database_create_tables_at_setup = False

Contributed by `@MarcBresson <https://github.com/MarcBresson>`_ in
`#​9228 <https://github.com/celery/celery/pull/9228>`_.

Bumps the npm_and_yarn group with 1 update in the / directory: [json5](https://github.com/json5/json5). Updates `json5` from 0.5.1 to 2.2.3
Release notes

Sourced from json5's releases.

v2.2.3

  • Fix: json5@2.2.3 is now the 'latest' release according to npm instead of v1.0.2. (#299)

v2.2.2

  • Fix: Properties with the name __proto__ are added to objects and arrays. (#199) This also fixes a prototype pollution vulnerability reported by Jonathan Gregson! (#295).

v2.2.1

  • Fix: Removed dependence on minimist to patch CVE-2021-44906. (#266)

  • New: Accurate and documented TypeScript declarations are now included. There is no need to install @types/json5. (#236, #244)

v2.1.2

  • Fix: Bump minimist to v1.2.5. (#222)

v2.1.1

  • New: package.json and package.json5 include a module property so bundlers like webpack, rollup and parcel can take advantage of the ES Module build. (#208)
  • Fix: stringify outputs \0 as \\x00 when followed by a digit. (#210)
  • Fix: Spelling mistakes have been fixed. (#196)

v2.1.0

  • New: The index.mjs and index.min.mjs browser builds in the dist directory support ES6 modules. (#187)

v2.0.1

  • Fix: The browser builds in the dist directory support ES5. (#182)

v2.0.0

  • Major: JSON5 officially supports Node.js v6 and later. Support for Node.js v4 has been dropped. Since Node.js v6 supports ES5 features, the code has been rewritten in native ES5, and the dependence on Babel has been eliminated.

  • New: The test framework has been migrated from Mocha to Tap.

items.title: Restore macOS process CPU and memory visibility
items.body:
## What changed

- Run Apple’s absolute `/bin/ps -axo pid=,pcpu=,rss=` beside every fresh osfacts process snapshot on Darwin, with no feature flag or capability gate.
- Use the native CPU/RSS values only for per-PID `U` facts or whole-source `E` facts that say the corresponding osfacts facet is unreadable. Readable osfacts values always win.
- Carry command-fallback provenance per process facet. Recovered CPU/memory values keep their numbers and gain a quiet `↩` in the table and process details; hover/accessibility text names `/bin/ps`.
- Keep Linux on the osfacts-only path and keep a failed/timed-out `ps` enrichment from rejecting the authoritative osfacts frame.
- Update the README’s observation, provenance, presentation, and limitation contracts.

## Why

Apple denies task-info reads for other users’ processes to ordinary binaries, so osfacts correctly reports their CPU and resident memory as unreadable. Apple’s privileged system `ps` can observe those two vital facts. The merged osfacts migration therefore left macOS fleet views with visibly incomplete process rows even though the host already provides a native recovery source.

## Design

The implementation follows the two-axis separation described in [The spacetime of code](https://kolu.dev/blog/hickey-lowy/):

- `darwinPs.ts` owns Apple command execution and wire-format parsing;
- `processUsageFallback.ts` owns the pure replacement and provenance policy;
- `proc.ts` owns poll concurrency and composition only;
- the shared process surface carries generic per-facet command provenance;
- the cell presenter owns the command-agnostic fallback marker.

This keeps native command volatility out of the osfacts projection, keeps unreadability policy out of the command adapter, and keeps `/bin/ps` knowledge out of the UI. The command retains the pre-osfacts reader’s bounded-child discipline: no shell, absolute executable, SIGKILL timeout, and an explicit large-output buffer.

## Validation

- Red-first parser and invocation tests.
- Red-first recovery tests for per-PID `U` facts, whole-source `E` facts, readable-value precedence, missing PIDs, Darwin failure, unconditional Darwin polling, Linux isolation, and per-facet provenance.
- Red-first presentation tests for keeping recovered values visible and exposing the command via hover/accessibility text.
- Live `/bin/ps` output shape checked on `zest`.
- Full browser-condition suite: 197 pass, 0 fail across 30 files.
- Workspace TypeScript typecheck passes.
- `nixpkgs-fmt --check` and `git diff --check` pass.

items.title: feat!: modernize toolchain and dependencies (P0)
items.body:
Implements **P0** from the production-readiness review: make the project compile and build again on a current toolchain.

## Changes

- **Dependencies**: `gmod` 10.2.2 → 17.0.1, `sysinfo` 0.22.4 → 0.39.6 (real version requirements, no more `\"*\"`). This drops the `ntapi 0.3.6` transitive that fails with hard error E0793 on any rustc since mid-2023 — the reason the locked tree stopped compiling. `lazy_static` is gone entirely, replaced by `std::sync::LazyLock`; sysinfo is built with `default-features = false, features = [\"system\"]`, which also sheds the rayon subtree.
- **Toolchain**: pinned `nightly-2026-08-01` (gmod-rs still requires nightly) with rustfmt/clippy components and all four release targets declared, so local and CI toolchains match. `#![feature(c_unwind)]` removed — stabilized since Rust 1.71.
- **Units/precision fix**: `get_memory()`/`get_swap()` now push Lua numbers (f64) in **bytes**. The old path cast through pointer-width `LuaInt`, which is i32 on the 32-bit builds and would overflow at 2 GiB the moment units became bytes. Doubles are integer-exact to 8 PiB. README updated accordingly.
- **Bug fixes**: `get_host_name` error no longer says "system version"; removed the leftover `"Goodbye from binary module!"` print on unload.
- **New in gmod 17**: client (`gmcl`) builds now call `restore_stdout()` on unload — required by gmod 17's stdout override, which otherwise crashes the game when the module unloads. The `gmcl` crate feature now properly forwards to `gmod/gmcl` so server builds don't compile the client machinery at all.
- **Hygiene**: error helper returns `!` to match `lua_error` semantics (call sites no longer read as fall-through bugs); dead `err!` macro arms removed; release profile added (`lto`, `codegen-units = 1`, `strip = \"symbols\"` — replaces the CI strip step); Cargo.toml gains description/license/repository metadata and `publish = false`.

## Breaking change

`get_memory()` and `get_swap()` return **bytes** (previously KiB). Conventional-commit footer is present so the release tooling bumps major (v2.0.0).

## Verification

- `cargo check` on all four targets (win32/win64/linux32/linux64), both realms (`sv` and `cl`/`--features gmcl`): clean
- `cargo clippy --all-targets` both realms: no warnings
- `cargo fmt --check`: clean
- `cargo build --release` both realms on win64: links, 205 KB stripped DLL

## Notes

- CI on this PR will fail — the existing workflow is still the broken pre-P1 pipeline (archived actions-rs, `::set-output`). P1 replaces it; this PR deliberately changes no workflows.
- Not runtime-tested in a live Garry's Mod instance yet; the GluaTest job planned for P1 covers that.

items.title: chore: move scripts and docs out of the repo root, fix broken references, and backfill the roadmap
items.body:
Moves the loose scripts and design docs out of the repository root, then repairs every reference that the move broke and fills in the Roadmap with what actually shipped.

The root had accumulated eight scripts, five markdown docs, and a stray `sequence-diagram.txt`. They now live in `scripts/` (which already existed) and `docs/`.

## Type of Change
- [ ] Bug fix
- [ ] New feature
- [ ] Enhancement
- [ ] Breaking change
- [x] Project / Infra

## What moved

| From (root) | To |
|---|---|
| `ARCHITECTURE.md`, `GLOBAL_DEPLOYMENT.md`, `PERFORMANCE.md`, `MACOS_APPLE_SILICON_INSTALLATION_GUIDE.md` | `docs/` |
| `sequence-diagram.txt` | `docs/deprecated/` |
| `cut_build_push_*.sh` (×4), `git_squash_all.sh`, `launch_chrome.sh`, `log_ssl_keys.sh`, `network_throttle.py` | `scripts/` |
| `rfc/rfc-1-q3-q4-2023-planning.md`, `start_dev.sh` | deleted |
| `.claude/settings.local.json` | untracked, kept on disk |

## Reference fixes

Every reference to a moved or deleted file was found by grepping the whole tree and re-pointed:

- `README.md` — four links to `ARCHITECTURE.md` / `PERFORMANCE.md` now point into `docs/`.
- `leptos-website/src/components/sections/Solutions.rs` — two `blob/main/ARCHITECTURE.md` GitHub URLs on the public site were dead; now `blob/main/docs/ARCHITECTURE.md`.
- `docs/MACOS_APPLE_SILICON_INSTALLATION_GUIDE.md` — `./launch_chrome.sh` → `./scripts/launch_chrome.sh`.
- `CONTRIBUTING.md` — the RFC Process section linked to the deleted `rfc/` directory. Replaced with an issue-and-Discord flow.
- `README.md` — the no-Docker config steps told you to run `./start_dev.sh`, which is deleted; they now say `make up`. Two table-of-contents entries pointing at removed sections (Manual Setup, Project Structure) are gone.

No CI workflow, Makefile, docker-compose file, or Helm chart referenced any of the moved files.

`.claude/settings.local.json` holds per-developer Claude Code permission state, so it is removed from the index and added to `.gitignore`. It stays on disk. The 11 shared agent definitions in `.claude/agents/` remain tracked, since `CLAUDE.md` instructs contributors to use that roster.

## Script fixes

Moving the scripts broke one of them and left four fragile:

**`launch_chrome.sh` was broken.** It derived its cert path from its own location, so after the move it looked in `scripts/actix-api/certs`:

```diff
-CERTSPATH="$SCRIPTPATH/actix-api/certs"
+REPO_ROOT="$( dirname "$SCRIPTPATH" )"
+CERTSPATH="$REPO_ROOT/actix-api/certs"
```

It also now does `mkdir -p "$CERTSPATH"` before generating a certificate — the `openssl req` call would have failed on a fresh clone with no `certs/` directory.

**The four `cut_build_push_*.sh` scripts only worked from the repo root**, since they pass `.` as the Docker build context and the Dockerfiles are still at the root. They now resolve the repo root from `$0` and `cd` there first, before the `git rev-parse` calls that derive the image tag.

`git_squash_all.sh` had usage comments referencing a nonexistent `./git-squash-all.sh` (hyphens); corrected to its real path. `log_ssl_keys.sh` and `network_throttle.py` have no path dependencies.

## Roadmap

The table listed five rows ending at Q2 2024, two of them still marked in-progress. It now covers Q3 2024 → Q3 2026, two deliverables per quarter (three for Q1 2026), including the pure-Rust VP9 codec (#884) and optional SQLite backend (#802).

Everything is sourced from this repo's history rather than written from memory: all 42 cited PR numbers were verified to resolve to real commits with matching subjects, and the Release column comes from actual `git tag` dates.

Two stale rows were dropped. `1.0.0 | Q2 2024 | 🔄 Production Release` never happened on that date — the tags show the 1.0.0 bump landed 2025-03-25, so it is now the Q1 2025 row. `0.8.0 | Q1 2024 | 🔄 Screen Sharing Improvements` had no commit tying it to that quarter; screen sharing is in the product and its most recent rework (#817) appears in the Q2 2026 row. Leaving either in-progress row above rows describing 2026 would have contradicted the table. The three 2023 rows were also sorted — they were jumbled (Q3, Q4, Q2).

One note on accuracy: the Q1 2026 adaptive-quality row cites #762, which was reverted (#771) and re-landed via #773. The code is live on this branch (`videocall-client/src/diagnostics/encoder_bitrate_controller.rs`).

Docs and shell scripts only — no application code changes, so no test surface. Verified manually:

- All four `cut_build_push_*.sh` scripts run against a stubbed `docker`, invoked both from `scripts/` and from `/tmp`; build context and Dockerfile resolve correctly in every case.
- `launch_chrome.sh` resolves to the real `actix-api/certs`, and the SPKI pipeline against the existing `localhost.der` produces a valid fingerprint.

items.title: docs: Evidence-safe loop coding — LOOP_CODING.md + README block
items.body:
# Evidence-Safe Loop Coding

> **Don't just prompt agents. Build loops that audit them.**

---

## The Problem with Vanilla Loop-Coding

Modern AI development is moving from one-shot prompts to **recurring agent loops**:
an agent gets a task, executes it on a schedule, reports back, repeats.

This is powerful. It is also dangerous.

A loop amplifies whatever is inside it. If the agent produces good, verified output — the loop
scales that. If the agent produces **Validation Theater** — synthetic tests, circular evidence,
self-confirmed success — the loop scales *that* too, silently, on autopilot.

```
Without evidence gates:

  Every 30 min → Agent runs → Agent creates synthetic data
              → Agent tests itself → Agent reports SUCCESS ✅
              → Loop repeats → You never see the gap
```

This is not automation. It is automated self-deception.

---

## What Evidence-Safe Loop Coding Adds

Every agent loop needs three things that vanilla loop-coding frameworks skip:

| Layer | What it does | Without it |
|---|---|---|
| **Evidence classification** | Labels every claim: `[VERIFIED-REAL]` vs `[VERIFIED-SYNTHETIC]` | Agent reports success on mock data |
| **Audit gate** | Blocks action if evidence is synthetic, round numbers, or self-authored | Deployed hallucination |
| **Memory update** | Records what the loop found, so next cycle doesn't repeat known-bad paths | Infinite retry of dead branches |

---

## Architecture

```
Loop Trigger (schedule / event / condition)
        ↓
  Agent Task (scoped, bounded)
        ↓
  Evidence Classification
  ├── [VERIFIED-REAL]   → proceed
  ├── [VERIFIED-SYNTHETIC] → block, require real data
  └── [UNKNOWN]         → escalate to human
        ↓
  Audit Gate
  ├── F1=1.000 or "100% success"? → Skeptic auto-trigger
  ├── Self-authored test? → [VERIFIED-SYNTHETIC], not valid
  └── Round numbers on real data? → flag
        ↓
  Human Approval  ←  (only when gate flags ambiguity)
  Auto Action     ←  (when gate passes clean)
        ↓
  Memory Update
  ├── Record what was found
  ├── Record what was NOT found (null results count)
  └── Update recurring mistake register
        ↓
  Next Cycle
```

---

## The Loop Spec Template

Before building any recurring agent workflow, fill this spec:

```markdown
# Loop Spec: [Name]

## Trigger
- Interval or event:
- Stop condition (required — loops must have exits):
- Max iterations before human review:

## Agent Task
- Input source (must be external, not self-generated):
- Allowed actions:
- Forbidden actions:

## Evidence Rules
- What counts as [VERIFIED-REAL] in this domain:
- What is automatically [VERIFIED-SYNTHETIC] (mock, seed, inline data):
- What must be marked [UNKNOWN] and escalated:

## Audit Gate
- Skeptic auto-trigger conditions (suspicious perfection, round numbers):
- What requires human approval before action:
- What can auto-proceed when evidence is clean:

## Memory Update
- What to record on success:
- What to record on failure (null results are data, not noise):
- Where results live (.claude/memory/ or project-specific):
```

---

## How This Repo Implements It

| Loop requirement | This repo's mechanism |
|---|---|
| Evidence classification | `rules/integrity.md` — evidence markers, `[VERIFIED-REAL]` hard rule |
| Synthetic detection | `hooks/validation_theater_guard.py` — detects inline synthetic test data |
| Skeptic auto-trigger | `hooks/skeptic_auto_trigger.py` — fires on F1≥0.9, round numbers, "all passed" |
| Audit gates | `hooks/pre_commit_guard.py`, `hooks/promotion_gate_guard.py` |
| Null result tracking | `null_results/INDEX.md` + `hooks/null_retroscan.py` |
| Memory update | `hooks/knowledge_librarian.py`, `hooks/session_save.py` |
| Human escalation | `rules/falsification-ladder.md` § Step 8a (skeptic gate before promote) |

---

## Relation to Langflow and Other Platforms

Platforms like [Langflow](https://github.com/langflow-ai/langflow) make it easy to **build** agent
workflows visually. They handle the loop mechanics well: triggers, routing, tool calls, API
deployment.

What they do not provide: **evidence discipline inside the loop**.

```
Langflow (or any loop platform) = where the agent runs
This repo = how to stop the agent from lying to itself while running
```

If you use Langflow or a similar platform, this methodology layers on top:
- Add evidence markers to your component outputs
- Wire the Audit Gate before any "action" node
- Add a null-result branch to capture what the agent did NOT find
- Require human approval when the gate flags suspicious perfection

---

## Anti-patterns

| Pattern | Why it breaks loops |
|---|---|
| Agent creates test data, then tests itself | Circular: every loop will succeed by construction |
| "100% success" with no external data source | Skeptic auto-trigger fires — flag immediately |
| No stop condition on the loop | Infinite retry of dead branches; null results accumulate silently |
| Memory not updated on null results | Loop loses the knowledge that path X is dead |
| Human approval only on failure | Gates only catch what you expected to fail; misses the unknown-unknowns |

---

## Quick Reference

```
Building a recurring agent loop?
  1. Write the Loop Spec (above) before touching code
  2. Confirm input source is EXTERNAL (not self-generated)
  3. Wire evidence classification before any action node
  4. Set skeptic auto-trigger thresholds (F1 > 0.9, "all passed", round numbers)
  5. Add null-result branch — null results ARE outputs
  6. Add stop condition — all loops must have exits
  7. Test the gate with a known-synthetic input: it must BLOCK
```

---

**See also:**
- [`rules/integrity.md`](../rules/integrity.md) — evidence markers and the Submission Gate
- [`rules/audit-verification-gate.md`](../rules/audit-verification-gate.md) — HIGH/MEDIUM claim verification protocol
- [`docs/anti-hallucination.md`](anti-hallucination.md) — standalone paste-in standard
- [`rules/falsification-ladder.md`](../rules/falsification-ladder.md) — full claim lifecycle

items.title: fix(autofill): refuse an unlock the extension's memory budget cannot survive
items.body:
# Summary

Addresses the expensive-KDF half of #57. An AutoFill extension runs under a memory limit far below the app's, and Argon2 allocates its full memory parameter in one block up front. The parser accepts up to 4 GiB there, so a database configured with a large Argon2 memory setting takes the extension down mid-unlock before any error can be produced — the reporter saw AutoFill do nothing at all while the same vault opened normally in the app.

The KDF parameters sit in the plaintext outer header, so the requirement is knowable before the derivation starts. `loadEntries` now pre-flights against `os_proc_available_memory` and fails with a message naming both numbers and the way out, instead of being killed with nothing to report. The silent QuickType path needs no change: its existing catch escalates to `.userInteractionRequired`, which re-runs the request with UI where the message is shown.

**What the check compares is deliberately narrow: the Argon2 memory parameter against the remaining budget, and nothing else.** Argon2 takes that parameter as a single allocation, so a parameter larger than what the process may still allocate cannot succeed whatever else the unlock would have gone on to do — arithmetic, not estimation. The decrypt and parse that follow are *not* priced in, even though they need memory: they belong to a later peak (the KDF block is freed before the payload is decompressed), so folding them in would compare against a budget no single moment of the unlock ever faces, and would start refusing large databases that open today. The two error cases are not symmetric — a false refusal breaks a working vault, while the bug being guarded against only breaks one that already fails — so the check refuses to guess. The file's own bytes are not counted either: the check runs after the file is in memory, so `os_proc_available_memory` has already deducted them.

`os_proc_available_memory` is `API_UNAVAILABLE(macos)` and reports 0 for a process under no limit; both cases skip the check. AES-KDF and an unrecognized KDF contribute nothing and are never refused. The header's memory parameter is attacker-controlled and is not range-checked until `deriveKey`, but it is compared rather than summed, so `UInt64.max` reaches the comparison intact with no overflow surface at all.

**Not a full fix for #57, so no closing keyword.** The check runs after the file is already in memory, so it covers the KDF allocation but not a database so large that reading it is itself fatal. That case needs a guard on the read and a second message before the header can be inspected; noted in `KeeForge/Services/AutoFill/README.md`.

# Changes

- `KeeForge/Services/AutoFill/AutoFillMemoryLimit.swift` — new: the budget comparison and the localized `BudgetExceeded` error. On both AutoFill allow-lists in `project.yml`.
- `AutoFillExtension/CredentialProviderCoordinator.swift` — pre-flight in `loadEntries` before the session key is created, plus a DEBUG-only `memoryBudgetOverride` so the path is testable without a device under real pressure.
- Both `Localizable.xcstrings` catalogs — new string in `en`, `de`, `fr`, `es`.
- `CHANGELOG.md` under `## Unreleased`, and the two folder READMEs.
- Tests: `KeeForgeTests/AutoFillMemoryLimitTests.swift` (new) and two coordinator tests covering the over-budget refusal and that a within-budget unlock still opens.

# Testing

```
xcodebuild test -project KeeForge.xcodeproj -scheme KeeForge \
  -destination 'platform=iOS Simulator,name=iPhone 17 Pro' \
  -only-testing:KeeForgeTests/AutoFillMemoryLimitTests \
  -only-testing:KeeForgeTests/CredentialProviderCoordinatorTests \
  -only-testing:KeeForgeTests/CredentialProviderPickerCreationTests \
  -only-testing:KeeForgeTests/LocalizationTests
```

- 87 tests, 0 failures. The unit tests pin both directions: an over-budget Argon2 block is refused and reported verbatim, while an exactly-fitting block, a vault whose file dwarfs the budget, AES-KDF with 100M rounds, an unrecognized KDF, and an unlimited process all pass untouched.
- `-only-testing:KeeForgeTests/KDBXCompatibilityTests` — 19 tests, 0 failures.
- `xcodebuild build -scheme KeeForgeMac -destination 'platform=macOS' CODE_SIGNING_ALLOWED=NO` — succeeds, covering the `#else` branch of `remainingBytes()`.
- `swift scripts/normalize-xcstrings.swift --check` — clean.

# Checklist

- [x] Updated `CHANGELOG.md` under `## Unreleased` (feature/bug-fix changes)
- [x] Ran `xcodegen generate` after adding/removing/moving source files
- [x] Updated the nearest folder-local `README.md` if the folder's map changed
- [x] Localized new UI strings in all shipped locales (`en`, `de`, `fr`, `es`) and ran `LocalizationTests`
- [x] Kept AutoFill extension target membership/imports in sync for shared code
- [x] Updated `KDBXCompatibilityTests` if parser/writer/save behavior changed — n/a, parser and writer behavior is unchanged; the suite was run as a regression check
- [x] Preserved accessibility identifiers or updated the affected UI tests — n/a, no UI structure changed

items.title: CC-005: state the growth policy, correct the latency range, build nothing
items.body:
> **Stacked PR 3 of 3 — merge last.**
> Based on `cc/004-persistence`, not on `main`. Order: #30 → #31 → **this**.
> Merging out of order will pull in DX-002, CC-003 and CC-004 unreviewed.

Closes `CC_001` O5 **as stated**. Pre-registration `43588944`.

**Status: PASS** — documentation and measurement. No eviction implemented, by design.

## How Part 0 resolved the gate

§3.1's first row made this part's scoping conditional on DX-002. The answer arrived in two pieces pointing different ways:

- **DX-002 returned Branch B** — the Study 010 runner's context was not bounded.
- **CC-003's G-E0 found the library bounded** — 0 turns over budget, p95 +18 chars.

So for `episodic`, eviction *is* a disk-and-latency policy after all — but on G-E0's authority, not on a plateau read off DX-002. **Scoped from DX-002 alone it would have been scoped wrong.**

## What grows

| Path | Grows with | Measured | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| Delivered context | turn count | +18 chars p95 over 1,000 turns | Bounded (G-E0) |
| Disk | turn count, linearly | 4,743 bytes/turn marginal; 4.8 MB at 1,000 turns | Cheap |
| Retrieval latency | store size, super-linearly | 190 ms at 1,000 candidates; exponent 1.25 | **Binding** |

Disk is 86% embeddings — 4,096 bytes of float32 against ~650 bytes of text. ~48 MB at 10,000 turns. Nothing there ends continuous operation.

Latency does. Clustering is **81%** of the cost at 1,000 candidates, up from 37% at 50, with its own exponent of 1.54.

## The correction

§3.1 quotes DR-002 as "~40 µs/candidate, exponent 0.96", projecting "~40 ms at 1,000 candidates and ~400 ms at 10,000". Measuring the same configuration on the same material to 1,000 candidates gives **190 ms** — about five times that projection.

**DR-002 is not wrong.** Its committed sweep is six rows from 20 to 119 candidates — its own report calls it "a 6x range in pool size" — and inside that range per-candidate cost is flat at 35–43 µs exactly as recorded. The projections extend that curve **84× beyond its last measured point**, and per-candidate cost stops being flat shortly after DR-002 ran out of data.

Two published statements corrected in `ERRATA.md`:

1. `episodic/README.md` claimed the sweep covered "20–3,000 candidates". It covered **20–119**. The 3,000 was a cumulative *character* figure from the DR-002 report's greedy-trace table, misread as a pool size.
2. The projections built on the 0.96 exponent are withdrawn, replaced with measurements to 1,000 candidates and clearly labelled projections above that.

**The practical consequence: the horizon is nearer than the pre-registration assumed** — seconds per query at 10,000 candidates, not the 400 ms §3.1 treats as the number that ends continuous operation.

## The policy, stated

**Unbounded retention. This version evicts nothing.**

§3.4 recommended shipping neither bounded-cost candidate generation nor archival in v0, on the grounds that building an eviction policy before anyone has hit the wall is speculative. That recommendation is followed, and §3.3's point stands: **stating the policy is the deliverable.**

Stated horizon: **comfortable to a few thousand episodes, unusable in an interactive loop somewhere before 10,000.**

### Why trimming is not the fix

The obvious move — drop low-similarity episodes to keep the pool small — is the one operation measured to break retrieval. Dropping the 19 lowest-cosine episodes from a 119-episode pool cost an entire domain and all known-optimum overlap, **despite 4 of the 5 optimum episodes surviving the cut**. The selector clusters over the pool, so tail removal reshuffles the objective rather than removing options (DR-002).

Any eviction policy must therefore be evaluated against **domain coverage**, not a similarity threshold. The candidate policy defaults to the full store; the trimming knob keeps its `unsafe_` prefix with the finding in its docstring.

### The open question, named as one

Latency is dominated by clustering, recomputed over the whole pool on every query. That is a caching and incrementality problem before it is an eviction problem, and it is out of scope here. ANN was already refuted at synthetic scale (bakeoff T5).

## Also in this PR: both corrections reach the library's limitations

A correction filed only in `ERRATA.md` is one the next reader of the README will not see. The library's limitations section now carries both failures the program's own gates caught — the confidence interval read as evidence of boundedness, and the scaling range quoted eight times wider than measured — with the transferable lesson stated plainly: **check the range a scaling number was measured over before relying on it.** Four tests keep the section from rotting.

## Deliverables (§3.5)

- [x] Measured disk growth per turn — 4,743 bytes/turn marginal
- [x] Latency curve to the largest store available, projection labelled
- [x] README growth section with the stated policy and the unsafe-trimming finding
- [x] `unsafe_` prefix retained on the trimming API
- [x] **No eviction implementation in v0** — asserted by tests scanning the package for eviction entry points and for `DELETE FROM episodes`

## Boundary

- One machine, one runtime, one quantization, one store. The absolute milliseconds are not portable; **the exponent and the clustering share are the transferable findings.**
- The latency curve is measured to 1,000 candidates because that is the largest store the program has. Everything above is a fitted projection — and a fitted projection is exactly what this part had to correct in DR-002's numbers. Treat it with the same suspicion.
- Disk growth uses a deterministic stub embedder. Vector width and row shape are identical to production, so the byte count is faithful.
- The horizon statement is about this configuration at a 32,000-character budget with 16 clusters. It is not a property of the design.

## Definition of done for the library (§5)

O1 enforced · O2 implemented · O3 measured · O4 guaranteed · O5 stated.

**O6 — runtime independence — remains open and unmeasured**, and the library README says so: every number is from one model, one quant, one machine.

## Checklist

- [x] Report committed with the pre-registration SHA in its header
- [x] Root `README.md` status line and study table updated
- [x] `AGENTS.md` digest entry (390 chars, under the 400 cap)
- [x] `ERRATA.md` updated — two published numbers changed
- [x] Memory files updated
- [x] Suite green: **1,011**

items.title: docs: publish cross-engine benchmark table and executed writeups
items.body:
## Intent Publish the project's benchmark results: (1) a cross-engine 'Benchmarks' table in the main README showing, per query class, where MySQL 5.7 workloads regress or improve on each migration candidate (5.7→8.0 and 5.7→MariaDB 10.11, Δp95 plus Δmean where the source reports emphasize it), with regressions visually distinct via plain-text-friendly markers (bold + sign, not color-only); (2) the three executed benchmark writeups ported into docs/benchmarks/ (2026-07-16-mysql80-general.md, 2026-07-16-mysql80-hugetext.md, 2026-07-16-mariadb.md) and linked from the table and from docs/quickstart.md. The writeups are faithful ports of internal executed reports, scrubbed of internal references; every number was transcribed exactly from the source reports and verified — numeric values in the table and writeups are ground truth from real runs and must not be 'corrected'. Required footnotes kept deliberately: the 8.0 general run was stock-charset (charset confound deliberate — baselines labeled latin1-5.7 vs utf8mb4-5.7); blob MB/s absolutes are not comparable across tool versions (sql-replay 0.2.0 vs 0.4.0 memory model); all numbers are WSL2 ratios, not production absolutes; MariaDB sql_mode behavioral diffs called out as the real migration gotcha. The story the table tells: 8.0's group-by/temp-table cliff (up to ~5x, tunable) vs MariaDB's -15% on the same class; blob transfer at par on both; per-statement overhead on tiny queries as 8.0's other loss. A prior run raised the ask-user finding 'quickstart-charset-alone-overclaim' about docs/quickstart.md; the user decided: attribute the ~5x GROUP BY slowdown to stock 8.0 defaults (utf8mb4 default + TempTable on-disk spill), NOT 'charset alone' and NOT 'largely charset-driven' — that decided fix is already applied as the branch's pipeline fix commit 4e8e2c3 (no-mistakes(review): reword quickstart GROUP BY slowdown attribution to stock defaults); the finding is resolved and must not re-surface. The remaining 'charset alone costs 5.7 about +68% p95' statements in README/mariadb writeup are a different, accurate measured claim (5.7-latin1 vs 5.7-utf8mb4 baseline pair) and are intentional. Docs-only change; code, tests, and lint untouched. ## What Changed - Added a "Benchmarks" section to the README with a cross-engine table showing per-query-class Δp95 (plus Δmean where the source reports emphasize it) for MySQL 5.7→8.0 and 5.7→MariaDB 10.11 migrations, with regressions marked bold-with-sign so they read without color; load-bearing footnotes cover the 8.0 general run's stock-charset baseline labeling, the cross-tool-version blob MB/s caveat, and WSL2 ratios-not-absolutes. - Ported three executed benchmark writeups into `docs/benchmarks/` (`2026-07-16-mysql80-general.md`, `2026-07-16-mysql80-hugetext.md`, `2026-07-16-mariadb.md`), linked from the README table and `docs/quickstart.md`; every number is transcribed from real runs. Also reworded the quickstart's ~5x GROUP BY slowdown attribution to stock 8.0 defaults (utf8mb4 + TempTable on-disk spill) rather than charset alone, and per pipeline review corrected the checksum-match claim to 14 deterministic of 16 checked fingerprints in the README and MariaDB writeup. - Noted the `docs/benchmarks/` executed-writeup convention in `AGENTS.md` (numbers come from real runs, never hand-edited; new runs get new dated files). Docs-only change: the pipeline confirmed no code was touched, all 47 relative links and every table/prose number cross-check against the source writeups, and both new sections render correctly under GitHub's markdown renderer. ## Risk Assessment ✅ Low: Docs-only change; the single prior finding (checked-vs-deterministic checksum count) was fixed as instructed in both files, all table numbers match their source writeups, and all cross-file links and anchors resolve. ## Testing Exercised the docs the way a reader would: checked every relative link and anchor (47/47 resolve), cross-checked every README benchmark table cell and prose number against the executed writeups (all match, including bold regression markers and the corrected 14-of-16 checksum count), confirmed the decided quickstart wording and scrubbing constraints, and captured GitHub-rendered screenshots of the table and a writeup — everything passes; cargo tests skipped as the diff contains no code. - Evidence: README Benchmarks section rendered as GitHub-flavored markdown (table, bold regression markers, footnotes) (local file: /tmp/no-mistakes-evidence/01KXNW5Z6V9GCMM5N2SYGYQD3Y/readme-benchmarks-render.png) - Evidence: MariaDB writeup rendered (header, verdict, general-workload results table) (local file: /tmp/no-mistakes-evidence/01KXNW5Z6V9GCMM5N2SYGYQD3Y/mariadb-writeup-render.png)

items.title: Add message search to the web front-end
items.body:
Implements a `/search` endpoint for the web interface that allows users to search messages across their accessible rooms by subject, sender, or message body.

## Summary

This adds full-text search capability to the web front-end, complementing the room list's limited "new/old/all" navigation. The implementation prioritizes security by ensuring the room set acts as the access control boundary—searches never widen what a user can already reach.

## Key Changes

- **New `http/src/web_search.cpp`**: Core search implementation with two distinct match paths:
  - Header search (subject/author): Single prepared statement over the entire store using `contains(lower(...), $1)` for case-insensitive matching without escaping concerns
  - Body search: Iterative message decoding (capped at configurable scan limit) since message bodies are often base64-encoded in `format_type 4` messages and cannot be efficiently queried at the SQL level

- **Access control via room enumeration**: Uses `citadel::ListRooms` and `RoomUnlocked` (the same helpers used by room list and `RequireUnlocked`) to build the searchable room set. Client-supplied `room=` parameters are ignored if outside this set, ensuring private rooms stay invisible, zapped rooms stay forgotten, and passworded rooms remain unsearchable until unlocked.

- **UI integration**:
  - Search box in page header with field selector (Subject or sender / Subject / Sender / Message text)
  - Optional date range filtering (since/until)
  - Configurable results per page and scan limit
  - "Search this room" link on room toolbars
  - Search link in sidebar

- **Configuration**: Added `qm_web_search_scan` config parameter (default 2000) to cap body search iterations, with the page reporting when the limit was hit rather than presenting partial results as complete.

- **Documentation**: Updated TODO.md, MEMORY.md, and README.md with search feature details and design rationale.

## Implementation Details

- Date bounds are parsed from `<input type=date>` and converted to UTC timestamps, with `until` made inclusive by adding 86399 seconds (end of day)
- Results are ordered newest-first with msgnum as tiebreaker for stable pagination
- Body search deliberately loads messages one at a time to avoid materializing all bodies simultaneously (which would include attachments and cause unbounded memory growth)
- All query string parameters are percent-encoded; room numbers are inlined from the enumerated set, never from client input

items.title: fix: stop review hints firing on prose, and let memory_update retype
items.body:
## What changed and why

Review hints were flagging memories whose text merely *contained* the trigger words. Measured against the live 751-memory corpus: **precision 0.65 → 0.79**.

### The defects

- **`waiting-on` matched any "waiting for" / "blocked on" anywhere in the body.** `"blocks forever waiting for EOF"` and `"waiting for first init container image pull"` flagged permanently. Both describe a mechanism, not a status.
- **Nothing checked quoting.** A memory *citing* `"expire 2026-06-29"` tripped the very signal it was documenting.
- **Date signals ignored `last_confirmed`.** A memory reconfirmed *after* the date it names, with the outcome written into the body, flagged forever.
- **Deprecated memories carried hints on the read surfaces** while `memory_stats` excluded them, so the two disagreed about the same memory.
- **`memory_update` had no `type` param**, so the sanctioned remedy for a misfiled memory (retype to a timeless type) was impossible through the MCP surface. With it unavailable, the observed workaround was to reword the prose until the flag cleared — which degrades the record while leaving the stale claim in place.

### The fixes

- `waiting-on` requires the wait to name an agent within 60 chars: a person, a PR/MR, a ticket key, or a named artifact. The other gated signals carry their own subject and get only the quoting filter.
- No signal fires inside quotes or backticks. Only `"` and `` ` `` delimit — a bare `'` is far more often a possessive (`Boomtastic's`) or contraction (`PR'd`), and treating it as a quote silenced ordinary prose.
- `expired-date` / `stale-as-of-date` defer to a `last_confirmed` that postdates the named date. Compared against **end-of-day**: a memory written on day X saying "as of day X" would otherwise suppress its own signal at birth.
- `_attach_review_hints` skips deprecated memories, matching `compute_review`.
- `memory_update` accepts `type`, validated against `MemoryType`. Retyping does not re-embed — the vector derives from title + content only.

## Cost, measured not assumed

A wait on an unnamed lowercase noun (`"waiting on the vendor"`) no longer fires. On the labeled corpus this silenced **3 false positives and 2 true ones**.

A dated-snapshot exemption was also built and scored, then **dropped**: it removed 7 false positives at the cost of **17 true ones** (recall 1.00 → 0.37), because dated session logs assert state that readers act on. Not shipped.

One methodology note worth keeping: the first benchmark counted deprecated memories and overstated the live backlog by ~46%. `compute_review` filters them; the ad-hoc script did not.

## `.ai/` files updated

| File | Change |
|---|---|
| `.ai/plans/status.md` | New entry for this pass incl. the measured numbers and the dropped-rule note |
| `.ai/memory.md` | Tool surface: `memory_update` accepts `type` |
| `.ai/specs/dataflow.md` | Lifecycle: retyping semantics, no re-embed |
| `.ai/specs/product-spec.md` | `memory_update` row |
| `docs/architecture.md` | Review Hints section rewritten: the three filters, and the stated cost |
| `README.md` | Tool table row |
| `CHANGELOG.md` | `[Unreleased]` Added + Fixed |

`.ai/specs/01-architecture.md` needs no change — no module added or removed, storage model unchanged (`type` was already a column). `.ai/standards/` and `.ai/agents/` need no change — no testing, code, database, or tech-stack convention moved.

## Tests

**334 pass** (+10), `ruff` + `black` clean. Every new test is pinned to a real corpus regression: the EOF and init-container false positives, the quoted-expiry case, the apostrophe bug, the same-day-confirmation edge, the deprecated-hint inconsistency, and the retype path.

items.body:
## Description

Audited every benchmark/economics claim in the repo against the code and evals that actually produce them, and closed the gaps found. No feature work — every number below was re-derived from a fresh, verified run against the final merged code, not guessed or copy-edited.

**Note on how this PR evolved:** the first commit fixed numbers measured against this branch's code. While preparing to push, the PR turned out to have a real merge conflict — `main` had drifted 985 commits ahead (several releases, substantial retrieval-path changes) and had independently drifted some of the *same* doc numbers on its own. Rather than resolve the conflict by picking one side, the second commit merges `main` in and **re-runs all three verification suites against the final merged code**, then propagates those numbers — which in some cases differ from what the first commit measured. The figures below are the current, final state.

**Economics (~1.6-3x, not 3-10x).** `docs/BUSINESS-CASE.md`'s own worked example already correctly derives ~1.6x end-to-end cost reduction, but 4 other surfaces (`HONEST-ASSESSMENT.md`, `about.html`, `Limits-and-Failure-Modes.md`, `vs-headroom.md`) still said "3-10x" — one of them self-contradicting its own page. Propagated the correct figure, and added an explicit disclosure that `neuralmind savings` (real logged usage vs. a fixed baseline) and `BUSINESS-CASE.md`'s formula (a what-if projection) are different measurements by design.

**Synapse-recall A/B (77.2%→83.3%, +6.1 pts).** Docs cited a stale "71.7%→83.3%, +11.6/+11.7 pts" in 16 files. A fresh run against the final merged code gives 77.2%→83.3%, +6.1 pts, deterministically — matching what `main` already had independently. Propagated everywhere. Also caught and fixed a real conflation: several surfaces mislabeled this synapse-recall delta as the *onboarding-lift* eval's number.

**Onboarding-lift eval (+0.9 pts, down from a previously-measured +6.5).** This is the most consequential finding. `evals/onboarding/runner.py` measures how much a committed team memory improves retrieval versus a cold agent — described in its own README as NeuralMind's "headline differentiator." Against this branch's pre-merge code it measured +6.5 pts (75.9%→82.4%). Against the fully merged code it's **+0.9 pts (81.5%→82.4%)** — the cold-path baseline itself got substantially better on `main`, which is a good thing architecturally, but it shrinks the memory layer's marginal contribution. Both measurements were real and deterministic at the time; noted honestly in `docs/wiki/Benchmarks.md` and `docs/wiki/Home.md` rather than smoothed over. Still clears the CI gate (lift ≥ 0).

**Public benchmark (79-100% recall, not a flat 100%).** `bench/public/report.md`/`results.json` were generated once at the benchmark's original commit and never regenerated since, despite `evals/public/manifest.json` growing to 4 repos (`requests`/`click`/`flask`/`rich`, 40 queries). Reran `python -m evals.public.run` against the final merged code: aggregate is **79-100% gold-file recall (93.75% mean, 90% found-rate), 44.9x-256.8x fewer tokens**. Also corrected an unconditional "beats ripgrep on both recall and cost" claim — NeuralMind ties ripgrep's recall exactly on `click` and `rich` (still wins cost on all 4). `click` is now the weakest repo (2 misses of 7) where an earlier run had zero — rewrote `docs/benchmarks/public.md`'s "Where NeuralMind loses" and "The corpus" sections to report this plainly, including the meta-point that this page's numbers moved twice in the same audit. Logged the regenerate-on-drift gap in `ROADMAP.md`.

**Left untouched, flagged instead of guessed:** the separate `codebase-memory-mcp` competitor-eval MRR numbers (off-by-default, needs an external binary this session didn't install) — noted inline in `public.md` as not yet re-verified against the expanded corpus.

## Type of Change

- [x] 📝 Documentation update

## How Has This Been Tested?

All verification below was run against the **final merged code** (after merging `main`):

- `python scripts/check_commercial_terms.py` — passes.
- `black --check` / `ruff check` on touched Python files (`neuralmind/cli.py`, `neuralmind/savings.py`, `neuralmind/__init__.py` — docstring/comment/version-conflict-resolution only, no logic changes) — pass.
- `pytest tests/test_benchmark_regression.py -v` — 5/5 pass.
- `pytest tests/` (full suite) — run against the merged tree.
- Every changed number was independently regenerated against the merged code: `python -m tests.benchmark.run` (4x, deterministic), `python -m evals.onboarding.runner --run` (3x, deterministic), `python -m evals.public.run` (full 4-repo run).
- Manual repo-wide `git grep` sweep after each fix confirmed no stale instances of the old numbers remain outside `docs/releases/` (historical, intentionally exempt) and `CHANGELOG.md`.

### Test Configuration

* **Python version**: 3.11.15
* **Operating System**: Linux
* **Test command**: `pytest tests/`

items.title: docs: memory profile + expanded README philosophy
items.body:
## Summary

Two related documentation changes:

### 1. Memory profile (`docs/memory-profile.md` + `scripts/peak-rss.sh`)

Replaces the README's handwave \"some workloads OOM memory-constrained hosts\" with concrete measured numbers.

| Workload | Peak RSS |
|---|---|
| sigil compile of any Plan-A2 program | ~63 MiB |
| cargo build --release -j 1 | 0.98 GiB |
| cargo test --workspace --no-fail-fast | 1.17 GiB |
| cargo build --release (parallel) | 1.56 GiB |

**Key finding:** sigil compile is constant-ish at 63 MiB regardless of input — hello, arith, fibonacci, higher_order all within 1 MiB of each other. Cranelift's load cost dominates; program complexity (e.g. closures) contributes negligibly. The pod-memory problem is a Rust/Cranelift build-time problem, not a sigil problem.

`scripts/peak-rss.sh` is the measurement tool itself (was previously untracked). Combines `/usr/bin/time -l` on the root with ps-based tree polling; reports max. macOS + Linux compatible.

### 2. README philosophical opener

Expands the one-paragraph \"Design philosophy\" into a structured set of sections capturing the framing from the design-doc conversation:

- **Why sigil exists** — every existing language was designed for humans; LLMs have different failure modes; push invariants into the grammar rather than downstream verifiers.
- **Design philosophy: fight the priors** — honest signatures, effect rows, no shadowing, explicit types on every binding, exhaustive matching, one way to do each thing. Each tied to the LLM failure mode it addresses.
- **Testability is a consequence** — effects-as-testing-seams, multi-shot replay testing.
- **What it looks like** — two code examples: fibonacci (Plan A2, currently working) and a Raise-handler snippet (Plan B, direction of travel).
- **What sigil deliberately is not** — honest tradeoffs: slower than C/Rust, verbose, anti-ergonomic for humans, not novel in any single feature.

Existing practical sections (Supported hosts, Quickstart, Diagnostics, Local verification + memory-profile pointer) preserved verbatim below. Status block updated to reflect Plan A2 complete.

## Scope

Docs only. No code changes, no non-negotiable impact, no plan-task deliverable.

## Reproduction of the memory numbers

```shell
# Build the compiler first.
cargo build --release

# Sigil compile measurements.
for ex in hello arith fibonacci higher_order; do
  scripts/peak-rss.sh ./target/release/sigil examples/$ex.sigil -o /tmp/mp_$ex
done

# Rust toolchain measurements (cold — cargo clean between each).
cargo clean && scripts/peak-rss.sh cargo build --release -j 1
cargo clean && scripts/peak-rss.sh cargo test --workspace --no-fail-fast
cargo clean && scripts/peak-rss.sh cargo build --release
```

`docs/memory-profile.md` documents the methodology, pod-feasibility matrix, and re-measurement cadence (Plan B, Plan C, GC replacement, major Cranelift upgrades).

items.title: Retrieval benchmark: associative-memory store vs. ColBERT-style late interaction
items.body:
## Summary

- Adds `scripts/bench-retrieval-vs-colbert.mjs` + `scripts/bench/`, a benchmark that runs our associative-memory retrieval organ (`emergence/store`: `buildStore`/`surface`, Hebbian sparse-code recall) against a ColBERT-style late-interaction retriever (MaxSim) and a pooled-cosine dense baseline, over the **same** frames and cue→source pairs.
- **Important caveat, spelled out in `scripts/bench/README.md`**: this sandbox's network policy allows pypi/npm but blocks `huggingface.co` — the only host for the real `colbert-ir/colbertv2.0` checkpoint. So `colbert-maxsim` is the real ColBERT *algorithm* (encode every token, score by MaxSim) run over WordLlama's static `l2_supercat` token embeddings (real, pretrained, MIT-licensed, ships inside the pip package — no network needed) rather than a fine-tuned contextual BERT. Treat it as a test of the late-interaction *architecture*, not a ColBERTv2 reproduction.
- Two evaluations, both recorded in `scripts/bench/RESULTS.md`:
  1. The 4 frozen `memory-golden.json` events (hand-verified ground truth) — a tier-discipline check. **All three systems correctly hit both engine-tier events and correctly GAP both model-tier ones (no leaks)** — the tier boundary this engine is built around held even against a semantic retriever.
  2. 60 auto-derived long-range verbatim-motif pairs per book, mined mechanically from `store.posting` (no hand curation) — Recall@1/5/10 + MRR at a much larger N than the frozen golden allows. Result: `engine ≥ colbert-maxsim ≥ dense-cosine` on both books (pg84 R@10 13/10/4 of 60; pg2600 R@10 4/3/2 of 60) — late interaction beats pooled-dense as ColBERT's own claim predicts, and the Hebbian sparse code holds a small edge at the range these motifs actually recur. All three are weak at long range.
- Updated `AGENTS.md` (symlinked as `CLAUDE.md`) with a new "Goldens and scorers" entry summarizing the above.
- No changes to `packages/engine` — purely additive benchmark tooling in `scripts/`.

## Test plan

- [x] `npm test` (full workspace suite) still passes — 35/35, unchanged since no engine code was touched.
- [x] `node scripts/bench-retrieval-vs-colbert.mjs pg84 pg2600` run end-to-end against real Frankenstein (`pg84.txt`) and War and Peace (`pg2600.txt`) text, twice, producing byte-identical numeric results both times (deterministic pipeline, no fabricated numbers).
- [x] Confirmed the existing frozen `scripts/score-memory-golden.mjs` still reports its documented baseline (engine 2/2 recalled, model-tier 2/2 gapped) against the same texts before building on top of it.

- Manual `vacuum()` still covers all tables

**V3 — Cost-based throttle (SHOULD ✅)**
- `VacuumCostConfig { enabled, cost_limit, cost_delay_ms, page_hit_cost, page_dirty_cost }` (Postgres-like GUC shape, default-on)
- `VacuumThrottle` stack-local accumulator; naps `cost_delay` when `accumulated >= cost_limit`
- Applied in both `vacuum_inner` (global) and `vacuum_table_inner` (per-table)
- `Engine::vacuum_cost_config()` / `set_vacuum_cost_config()`

**V4 — Whole-table compaction (SHOULD ⏸ DEFERRED)**
- Relocating live tuples changes RowIds → every secondary-index entry must be re-pointed atomically
- Crash-safe bracketing requires a new multi-page compaction WAL record (heap page + all index pages in one redo/undo unit) — a `FORMAT_VERSION` bump
- Per-page `compact_page` (M10.d) already handles intra-page dead-slot reclamation; V4 is cross-page defragmentation only
- Deferred with dated note in `docs/backlog/27_vacuum_per_table.md` §V4

## Benchmark measurements

| Scenario | Result |
|---|---|
| Bloat: 200 rows × 10 churns → vacuum_table | 2000 dead → 2000 reclaimed; cold bystander table = 0 reclaimed |
| Throttle tight budget (cost_limit=50, 2 ms nap) | ~121 ms |
| Throttle unthrottled | ~12 ms |
| Throttle overhead ratio | ~10× at tight budget; negligible at default (cost_limit=200) |

items.title: docs(audit) 2/4: the removal runbook that leaves debris, and four docs the calendar outgrew
items.body:
Pass **2 of 4** from the `/doc-audit` run — the remaining code↔doc drift. 11 files, docs only, no ALWAYS-set paths.

Every claim below was verified against source, not against another doc.

## The removal runbook that leaves debris

`context/calendar/remove-it.md` is a **runbook**, so each stale count is a broken removal, not a typo. Nine of them, all the same shape — a later phase invalidated a hard-coded number:

| Where | Said | Actual |
| --- | --- | --- |
| step 9 | delete 4 schema files, "remove all **four** lines from `schema/index.ts`" | **five** exports — omits `calendar-recurrence-dates`, **whose table the runbook's own SQL drops** ⇒ you're left with a module exporting a dropped table |
| step 9 | delete 2 integration tests | **four** exist |
| step 5 | 5 locale keys + "those **five** members" of `SENTENCE_KEYS` | **six** — `calendarReminder` left behind breaks the `satisfies Record<Exclude<…>>` guard that step relies on |
| step 6 | "remove **every** calendar entry from `coverage.include`" | omits `src/lib/calendar-reminders.ts` |
| step 7 | e2e helper list | omits `getEventReminders` |
| step 12 | clean "**the two attendee imperatives** at the bottom of that leaf file" | `packages/db/AGENTS.md` now ends in **four reminder** imperatives |
| header | "**three tables**" | six + a view |
| `:199` | "the **four** `DROP TABLE`s … added by `0020`, `0021` and `0023`" | **six**, spanning `0024` and `0025` too |
| `:13` vs `:190` | "five `calendar_*` members" vs "the other **six** types" | six total — and the two lines contradicted each other |

Fixed by **removing the counts where a count was never the point** — "every `./calendar*` export", "every calendar imperative in that leaf", "grep it rather than trusting this enumeration". Re-fixing the numbers would just guarantee the next phase invalidates them again.

Step 12 also now names `docs/README.md` and `BACKLOG.md`, which this PR and its predecessor gave calendar content. **A removal step that doesn't know about a doc we just wrote is drift we authored ourselves** — that pairing was a contrarian catch.

## `ARCHITECTURE.md` omitted the calendar entirely

The section that *enumerates* which `(dashboard)` surfaces are real-not-scaffold listed `/dashboard`, `/account`, `/organization` — and silently skipped `/calendar`. All five calendar routes were documented only inside `context/calendar/`, so the route map an agent is told to load *when adding features* didn't know they existed.

That includes **`/rsvp/[token]`** — the repo's only public, token-authenticated surface, and a route *handler* rather than a page. It now carries the gate for each route and why that one must stay outside the proxy matcher and the dashboard gate. `/admin/audit` got a pointer too.

## `DATABASE.md` denied what its own leaf file teaches

Its calendar heading stopped at `0023`, so `0024`/`0025` and both reminder tables appeared nowhere — while `packages/db/AGENTS.md` carried four reminder imperatives. The leaf was teaching things the owning doc said didn't exist.

Adds the invitations + reminders section, including why dropping the `anchor` CHECK is **half** the change: the sweeper windows on the occurrence's *start* instant, so an end-anchored reminder would silently never fire. (Tracked on the Calendar Phase 6 row filed in #27.)

## Two leaf `AGENTS.md` files

- `@repo/email` claimed to import `@repo/validators` — **it has no such dependency at all**.
- `@repo/jobs` listed two coverage-include entries; there are three. `reminders/sweep.ts` is named rather than globbed on purpose, and the leaf now says why.

## Also

`services/jobs.md` never named `calendar-invitation`, `calendar-reminder-email` or `calendar-reminder-notify` — it said the sweeper "is the only handler that ENQUEUES" without saying into what. `CONVENTIONS.md`'s file map missed `goodbye`/`accept-invitation/[id]` and two `api/` handlers (verified against the tree — this was the one claim I'd flagged as asserted-not-verified when the plan went to review). `SECURITY.md` still cited the installed Next as 16.2.11.

**`docs/archive/README.md` had fallen a pass behind its own rule** — *"Adding a file here updates this table in the same commit"* — with the twelfth audit report on disk and unindexed. Its `PHASE_HISTORY.md` row also omitted three later archived sections that `PROJECT_STATUS.md` links to by anchor. And `docs/README.md` never listed `context/calendar/` at all.

## Verification

`docs:sanity` (incl. the init-app anchor guard added in #27) · `biome check` · `lint` · `type-check` · `knip` · `lint:deps` — green. Docs-only diff: no source, no schema, no test changes, so build/test baselines are unaffected and CI arbitrates.

Both `PROJECT_STATUS.md` rows measured against the current ≤200-char rule: **194** and **191**.

## Contrarian disposition

No new review run: this PR carries **no** CLAUDE.md ALWAYS-set path (the `CONVENTIONS.md` edits are in **§ File Structure Within `apps/web/src`**, not **§ Agent tooling**, which is what the policy scopes to — owner-ruled section-scoped-as-written this session). Its content was reviewed as part of the audit plan that produced #27; the two findings contrarian raised against *this* slice were both folded here:

- **C6** — adding `context/calendar/` to `docs/README.md` creates new drift unless `remove-it.md` step 12 learns about it. **Paired in this PR.**
- **C6b** — step 12's *"the two attendee imperatives"* describes a leaf that no longer exists. **Fixed, count-free.**
- **c1** — the `CONVENTIONS.md` `(auth)`/`api` route claim was flagged asserted-not-verified. **Verified against the tree before writing it**, as promised.

## Still queued

**2c** — ledger + hot path: the seven remaining untracked deferrals, the ≤200→~250 row rule (owner-approved), ~52 lines of `PROJECT_STATUS.md` prose that duplicates canonical homes, memory slimming. **2d** — showcase currency: 26 stale numbers, and the entire calendar program absent from all 13 guide chapters and every slide.

items.title: perf: stream large session parses, attest release provenance, de-flake TUI tests
items.body:
Follow-up work on three items deferred from #28, plus a code-review + `/simplify` hardening pass. **All gates pass locally — lint clean, both typechecks clean, 195 tests pass (stable across repeated runs), full build succeeds.**

## 1. Streaming JSONL parse (`src/core/parser.ts`)

`parseSessionFile` previously did `Bun.file(path).text()` then `split("\n")`, holding the whole file as one string *and* its line array in memory alongside the parsed events — a real OOM risk for hundred-MB sessions.

It now reads the file as a byte stream and parses line-by-line; only the parsed events (which the caller needs anyway) plus one decode buffer are resident. Per-line logic is factored into a shared `parseLine`, so the streaming and in-memory (`parseSessionText`) paths can't drift.

Hardened after review:
- Line fragments are reassembled through an **array joined once per completed line (O(n))** rather than a growing `buf += chunk` (which was O(n²) when a single record spans many chunks). The common case — a line wholly within one chunk — stays allocation-free.
- Handles chunk-boundary splits, CRLF, and a missing final newline, with line numbers matching the in-memory parse.
- Tests: streamed-vs-in-memory equivalence, a 5000-line multi-chunk file with a malformed line mid-stream, a 300KB single line spanning chunks, CRLF, scalar lines, and rejection on a missing file (a behavior callers rely on).

## 2. Release build-provenance attestation (`.github/workflows/release.yml`)

The same-job `SHA256SUMS` manifest proves integrity but not origin. Added `actions/attest-build-provenance` to sign each binary with the workflow's OIDC identity — unforgeable from inside the job — tying every artifact to the exact run and commit that built it. Adds `id-token: write` + `attestations: write`; README documents `gh attestation verify cc-analyzer-linux-x64 --repo yorch/cc-analyzer`.

## 3. De-flake the TUI tests (`test/tui/**`)

All 7 Ink component test files used fixed `setTimeout` sleeps (20–100ms) after each keypress before asserting — too short flakes on a loaded runner, too long wastes wall-clock. Converted all 25 sites to poll the rendered frame for the exact condition each test checks, via a new shared helper (`test/helpers/tui.ts`: `waitForFrame` / `waitForFrameGone` / `waitFor`). Assertions unchanged.

Fixed in review: the sessions-view nav test polled/asserted `"sessions"`, which is always present in the nav rail, so it never actually verified the view switch — it now asserts the fixture session title, which renders only on that view.

One deterministic `setTimeout(0)` macrotask yield remains in `session-detail.test.tsx`: `SessionDetailScreen` subscribes `useInput` on a post-commit effect and Ink doesn't buffer input arriving before a handler is registered, so the first keypress needs one tick to land. A re-send-until-visible helper was considered and rejected — several keys there are non-idempotent (`j` next-turn, `Tab` toggle-focus, `Enter` expand) and re-sending would corrupt state. It's a single documented yield, not a load-tuned delay, verified stable across repeated full-suite runs.

Docs (README, CLAUDE.md) updated: streaming vs in-memory parse paths, and the attestation step.

items.title: release: ship PRs #88-#93 (local-model reliability, tool validation, chat mode)
items.body:
Rolls up six reviewed PRs onto one branch. Each was read for correctness before merging; conflicts between them were resolved by hand.

## Included

| PR | Change |
|----|--------|
| #88 | Ollama path survives small-model protocol slips (text-written tool-call recovery, empty-completion retry, malformed-arg repair, turn diagnostics, actionable path rejections) |
| #89 | Tool input property **type** validation, not just required-field presence |
| #90 | Unfinished subagent runs return an error instead of `(sub-agent produced no output)` |
| #91 | Bounded, configurable, actionable Ollama request waits |
| #92 | `anvil chat` interactive mode; provider selection extracted to `commands/provider.rs` |
| #93 | Dogfood alignment findings |

## Conflict resolutions (not verbatim from any single PR)

- **`OllamaProvider` (#88 x #91).** Kept both `temperature` (#88) and `request_timeout` (#91). The timeout is applied **per request**, not on the shared `Client`, so there is one timeout authority rather than layered ones. A timeout propagates immediately out of `complete_once`, so the empty-response retry loop does not stack three waits.
- **Default timeout 60s -> 120s.** #88 deliberately raised the hard-coded client timeout to 120s for cold local model loads; #91 kept 60s only because it was preserving the existing value while adding `--ollama-timeout-secs`. Took #88's empirical bound now that #91 makes it overridable. README updated to match.
- **`--temperature` (#88 x #92).** #92 deletes the `run.rs` block that #88 attached `--temperature` to, which would have left a dead flag. Moved it onto the shared `ProviderArgs`, so `run` and `chat` both accept it.
- **#93 doc.** The report only referenced the episodic-memory benchmark contamination in a passing clause, and attributed it to #88 as already fixed. It is not fixed. Rewritten as an explicit standing finding — see below.

## Standing finding recorded in `FEEDBACK_REPORT.md`

`anvil run` injects up to 5 goal-matching past episodes into the system prompt on every invocation (`Agent::build_system_prompt_with_memory`, `memory.search(goal, 5)`), from a single per-user SQLite DB under `$HOME`. `--session` does not scope it and no flag reports it.

Any benchmark looping `anvil run` over fixed goals therefore scores run *k* with runs *1..k-1* of the same goal pasted into its prompt. **This withdraws the earlier local fine-tune numbers** — they measured accumulated memory, not model capability, and must not be cited before a re-run under an isolated database.

## Verification (local, Rust 1.86)

- `cargo build --release` — ok
- `cargo test --all` — **115 passed, 0 failed**, 1 ignored
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings` — clean (matches CI)
- `cargo fmt --all -- --check` — clean
- Binary smoke test under an isolated `$HOME`: `anvil run --provider echo`, `anvil chat` multi-turn + `/exit`, `--temperature` and `--ollama-timeout-secs` present on both subcommands, `--ollama-timeout-secs 0` rejected.

items.title: docs: modernize Claude/Cowork templates for current AI workflows
items.body:
## Summary

Modernizes the Claude/Cowork governance template layer while leaving the website material untouched.

## Scope

This PR updates only Markdown template/governance files. It does **not** change website implementation, assets, HTML, CSS, JavaScript, or research-site material.

## Core repositioning

Moves the templates from the older framing:

> Claude starts cold every session, so these templates provide memory.

To the current framing:

> Claude may have project files, memory, connectors, Cowork-style file workflows, and background tasks. Use native features for convenience, but use explicit governance artefacts for authority, continuity, repair, truth, and auditability.

## Changes

- Adds `MODERN_CLAUDE_NOTE.md`.
- Adds `ADOPTION_LEVELS.md`.
- Adds `TEMPLATE_STATUS.md`.
- Adds `2026_RELEVANCE_AUDIT.md`.
- Modernizes `README.md` as the current front door for Claude/Cowork templates.
- Updates `RUNNING-DOCUMENT.md` as an authoritative project-state file rather than a paste-every-session memory workaround.
- Updates `SESSION-START-PROTOCOL.md` into a modern context-check protocol.
- Updates `CANONICAL-NUMBERS.md` for modern project files, linked sources, and memory conflicts.
- Updates `FAILURE-RECOVERY.md` for stale memory, connectors, Cowork file edits, and background task drift.
- Updates `PARTNERSHIP-AGREEMENT.md` for current Claude collaboration boundaries.
- Updates `TRUTH-PROTOCOL.md` while preserving anti-sycophancy logic.
- Updates `FOLDER-STRUCTURE.md` as advanced Cowork/agentic file governance rather than default setup.

## Guardrails

- No website material changed.
- No site assets changed.
- No HTML/CSS/JS changed.
- No research claims changed.
- No templates deleted.
- Claude/Cowork remains supported, but the templates are now clearly modular and risk-calibrated.

## Why

Claude/Cowork and modern AI workflows have moved quickly. The templates are still useful, but their practical role has changed: they should govern increasingly capable AI workspaces rather than assume every session starts from zero.
