items.title: chore(release): v1.4.0 gap-evident completeness
items.body:
## v1.4.0: gap-evident completeness

Minor release.

Authorization receipts can now carry an optional completeness block: a per-boundary sequence number and a running count, both signed under the same receipt signature and assigned gap-free at issuance. A dropped receipt inside a declared coverage boundary becomes a provable gap from the held receipts alone, with no appeal to the issuer's logs.

What is in it:

- Optional `completeness` block on authorization receipts (seq + runningCount), off by default. Coverage-free receipts and the existing conformance vectors stay byte-identical.
- `vaara verify-contiguity`: reads a receipt stream and reports every boundary whose sequence numbers skip, naming the missing range.
- Public `contiguity_v0` conformance vectors with an independent checker, so a third party can confirm the gap math without running Vaara.
- `SPEC.md` grammar updated for the completeness block and contiguity.
- Root-agnostic README and SPEC; `docs/PRIOR_ART.md` current as of this release.

Honest limit, documented in the spec, the test, and the vector README: contiguity catches a drop between two held receipts, not a truncated tail. Numbers run in memory at the chokepoint. Binding the running count into the timestamp anchor is deferred to a later release.

Full suite green: 1900 passed, 13 skipped.

items.title: perf: resolve the revalidateActive sweep in one batched read
items.body:
## What

The reconnect sweep did a per-key `load()`. It now snapshots the active set and resolves it through the existing `loadAll` — one `SourceOfTruth.readAll` instead of N `read`s.

## Why it matters more than the per-key numbers suggest

`load()` checks memory first, so the storage cost was already per *non-resident* key rather than per key. That sounds like it blunts the problem, but it points the other way: the reconnect this sweep exists for follows a process resume, which is exactly when memory has been shed and **every** active key is a miss. The path most likely to be cold was the one issuing N sequential reads.

Stores that leave `readAll` at its per-key-loop default see the same number of reads as before. Ones that override it — the SQLDelight adapter's `IN` clause, or your own — now serve the whole sweep in a single query.

## Why this is low-risk

`loadAll` is not new and not a parallel implementation: it is the batched twin `getAll`/`streamMany`/`prefetchAll` already go through, and its KDoc spells out that each miss is fenced exactly as `load` does — epoch captured before the read, re-checked under `commitGuard` with a memory re-read, same `sequencer`-based residual-hydration guard. So staleness judgement, fencing and hydration semantics are unchanged; only the number of storage round-trips moves.

Iterating a snapshot of `activeKeys` rather than the live map also makes the keys judged identical to the keys read, which the per-key loop didn't guarantee.

## Verification

- **New test `the sweep resolves every active key in one batched read`.** It uses a `SourceOfTruth` that *overrides* `readAll` and counts both entry points — the default implementation loops over `read`, which would hide the very thing being asserted — with `memoryCache { maxEntries = 1 }` to force the misses. Asserts one `readAll` and zero `read`s. I confirmed it catches the regression: restoring the per-key `load()` fails this test and only this test (18 tests, 1 failed).
- `./gradlew :aquifer-core:build :aquifer-test:build :aquifer-persistence-file:build :aquifer-okhttp:build :sample:build` green, detekt and `apiCheck` included.
- **`./gradlew :aquifer-core:lincheckTest` green (9m21s).** This PR was raised while that run was still going and previously said so; the run has since finished clean.
- No public signature moved, so no `apiDump`.

## Scope

This is the **read-side** part of the roadmap's `revalidateActive` item, after the per-stream `maxAge` fix in #83. Still open, and deliberately not attempted here: batching the sweep's *fetches*. That one is harder — a batched refresh has to preserve per-key single-flight, fencing and negative-cache behaviour, which `getAll`'s transport already does, so the work is routing the sweep through it rather than inventing a second path. The roadmap item now says exactly that.

README (the list of paths that batch through `readAll`) and `CHANGELOG.md` are updated here.

items.title: feat(catalog): item 25 — multi-page catalog, lift ~8 KiB HeapFull ceiling
items.body:
## Summary

Closes the single-page ~8 KiB catalog ceiling that item 23 (storage service) had to work around by dropping a column and front-loading all DDL.

**Root cause:** `Catalog::persist` wrote every `TableDef` + `TableStats` as one JSON blob into a single slotted page. Any blob > ~8 KiB failed with `HeapFull`.

**Fix:** multi-page chain with in-band magic detection:
- Each catalog page's slot-0 payload = 4-byte LE magic (`CATALOG_CHAIN_MAGIC = 0xC0DA7A10`) + 4-byte `next_page_id` + JSON chunk (max 8128 bytes/page)
- `persist`: allocates all N pages up front, WAL-logs them in **one mini-txn**, then flips `catalog_root` as the single atomic commit point
- `load`: if first 4 bytes = magic → follow chain; else → legacy raw JSON (old blobs open unchanged)

## Design decisions (committed before code — see `docs/backlog/25_multipage_catalog.md`)

1. **No `FORMAT_VERSION` bump (D9 honored):** magic first byte = 0x10 ≠ `{` (0x7B) — formats are unambiguously distinguishable without any version field
2. **Crash safety:** write-new-chain-then-flip; crash before the `catalog_root` control-file write leaves the old catalog intact; crash after = new chain is WAL-recovered. P33 verifies this.
3. **D5 compliance:** all N pages WAL-logged (`log_insert`) before `pool.write_page`, same discipline as before, extended across N pages in one mini-txn

## Before / after

| | Before fix | After fix |
|---|---|---|
| Max schema | ~18 cols across 3 tables (8 KiB) | Unlimited (bounded only by pool) |
| item-23 original layout (objects 11 cols + DLQ 8 cols) | `HeapFull{8883}` at `CREATE TABLE` | Creates, persists, reopens, queries ✓ |
| 100 tables × 20 columns | `HeapFull` | Succeeds, multi-page chain ✓ |
| `ANALYZE` after 3 000 rows | `HeapFull{9651}` | No overflow ✓ |
| 30 tables with `SERIAL`, 50 inserts each | `HeapFull` | No overflow ✓ |

## Test plan

- [x] `cargo test -p unidb --lib`: **406** (was 402; +4 catalog unit tests: `multipage_catalog_roundtrip`, `catalog_just_over_page_boundary`, `legacy_single_page_catalog_backward_compat`, `item23_original_schema_no_heap_full`)
- [x] `cargo test -p unidb --test crash`: **35** (was 34; +P33 `p33_crash_mid_multipage_catalog_write_old_catalog_intact`)
- [x] `cargo test -p unidb --test multipage_catalog`: **4** new integration tests (item-23 original layout, 100-table wide schema, ANALYZE-after-inserts, SERIAL-inserts)
- [x] `cargo clippy -p unidb -p unidb-storage -p unidb-dispatch --all-targets -- -D warnings`: clean
- [x] `cargo fmt --all -- --check`: clean
- [x] **No `FORMAT_VERSION` bump** — old single-page catalogs open unchanged (backward-compat test passes)
- [x] **No §3 locked decision reopened**
- [ ] Note: `unidb-logical` has a pre-existing compile error in its test helper (missing `Event` fields `before`/`after`/`ts_ms` added by item 29) — not caused by this change; reproducible on main before this branch.

## Docs updated

- `docs/backlog/25_multipage_catalog.md`: status → SHIPPED (design decisions recorded)
- `docs/backlog/backlog_index.md`: row 25 → ✅
- `docs/design/storage_service.md`: §4 note that the ceiling is lifted (item-23 workaround can be relaxed)
- `docs/design/engine_design.md`: §4.6 chain format description + version footer
- `README.md`: item 25 row in milestone table
- `PROGRESS.md`: full entry with before/after numbers
- `MEMORY.md`: current state

Relates to: item 23 (`docs/design/storage_service.md` §4 correction that first documented the ceiling), item 10 (durable FSM removed the page-list part of this blob; this removes the remaining TableDefs + TableStats part).

items.title: feat(android): native liquid glass on Android 13+ via AGSL shader

labels.name: new feature
labels.description: New feature

labels.name: android
labels.description: Android only

labels.name: performance
labels.description: Performance detail

items.body:
## Summary

`LiquidGlassView` now renders **real native liquid glass on Android 13+** instead of falling back to a tinted blur. The effect is the [AndroidLiquidGlassView](https://github.com/QmDeve/AndroidLiquidGlassView) AGSL shader (refraction, dispersion, blur and tint, all on the GPU), fed by the same battle-tested backdrop-capture model the library already uses for `BlurView`. On Android < 13 (and iOS < 26) the component keeps the existing `BlurView` fallback.

This PR also carries the ProgressiveBlurView fixes from the base branch (see below). Closes #119.

## Android liquid glass

### How it works

- **Shader, not widgets.** Only the MIT-licensed AGSL shader from AndroidLiquidGlassView is used, vendored into `res/raw` with its license header. The library's widget classes record the bound backdrop source with `target.draw()` on a hardware `RecordingCanvas`; with an RN ancestor as the source (the only general choice in an RN hierarchy) that recording transitively references the glass view's own `RenderNode`, creating a cyclic render tree that stack-overflows the render thread (`RenderNode::prepareTreeImpl` infinite recursion — reproduced and verified). The upstream demo only ever binds a *sibling* container, which RN cannot guarantee. The published AAR also requires `compileSdk 37+`, which AGP 8.9.1 cannot consume.
- **Cycle-free capture.** The backdrop is captured software-side from the nearest `react-native-screens` `Screen` (or `ReactRootView`) into a **reused half-resolution bitmap**, self-excluded via a `draw()` guard, refreshed at ~30 fps by an attach-scoped ticker. A flat bitmap holds no node references, so a render-tree cycle is impossible by construction — the same model `ReactNativeBlurView`/QmBlurView already proved safe.
- **GPU rendering.** The bitmap feeds a standalone `RenderNode` carrying the `RuntimeShader` `RenderEffect` chained with a backdrop blur, so the whole glass look runs on the GPU.

### API mapping (unchanged public API)

| Prop | Android behavior |
|---|---|
| `glassType` | `'clear'` → light backdrop blur, `'regular'` → frosty backdrop blur |
| `glassTintColor` / `glassOpacity` | shader-modulated tint using the exact iOS formula (`tintAlpha × glassOpacity`) — no scrim, no alpha cap |
| `isInteractive` | iOS-style press-scale animation |
| `borderRadius` (+ per-corner) | drives the shader's lens geometry (uniform base) + per-corner outline clipping |
| `ignoreSafeArea`, `reducedTransparencyFallbackColor` | iOS-only no-ops |

React children mount directly into the wrapper; the capture guard skips the whole subtree, so children are never refracted into their own backdrop.

### Platform gating

`RuntimeShader` requires API 33, so the JS gate renders native glass on **iOS 26+ / Android 13+** and the `BlurView` approximation everywhere below — both branches covered by new Jest cases.

### Measured performance (Galaxy A52s, Android 14)

The glass screen is statistically indistinguishable from the app's neutral baseline: ~173 MB native heap, **flat** over time (the capture bitmap is reused, so there is no allocation churn / GC sawtooth). For contrast, the first backend evaluated for this feature ([Liquid-Glass-Android](https://github.com/QWEA0/Liquid-Glass-Android), integrated in the first commit and replaced in the second) cost **+105–143 MB** of native heap with a ~38 MB GC sawtooth on the example screen (20 glass views, API 35 emulator) — its CPU pipeline holds three full view-sized displacement maps per view and re-captures full-resolution backdrops every frame.

### Docs

- `liquid-glass-view` page: Android 13+ platform behavior, plus a prominent **"use it wisely on Android"** note — liquid glass is not a native Android concept, every glass surface pays real capture/memory cost, prefer a few well-placed surfaces; includes the API 33 requirement and automatic fallback.
- `installation`, `liquid-glass-container`, `props-reference`, prop tables and README updated (bundled shader is attributed; no new Gradle dependency).

## Also included (from the base branch)

- `fix(android)`: make the default progressive blur visible and scope its DST_IN mask to the internal BlurView (children no longer fade), fix the horizontal gradient directions (#119)
- `fix`: unify `ProgressiveBlurView` `startOffset` semantics across platforms (#119)
- `docs`: document the Android blur backend behavior and unified `startOffset`

## Verification

- `yarn typecheck`, `yarn lint`, `yarn test` (40 tests, including the new Android 13+ / <13 gate cases)
- Example app built and run on a Pixel emulator (API 35) and a physical Galaxy A52s (API 34): glass renders with edge refraction, live backdrop under scrolling and background changes, correct rounded/pill clipping, stable across navigation remounts, clean logcat
- Memory profiled with `dumpsys meminfo` (numbers above)


<!-- This is an auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->
## Summary by CodeRabbit

- **New Features**
  - Added native liquid-glass effects for Android 13+ with tint, opacity, refraction, rounded corners, and interactive press scaling.
  - Older Android versions continue using enhanced blur fallbacks.
- **Improvements**
  - Refined progressive blur gradients, masking, rounded-corner clipping, and `startOffset` behavior across platforms.
  - Improved Android backdrop capture and Web blur rendering consistency.
- **Documentation**
  - Updated platform requirements, performance guidance, fallback behavior, migration notes, and Android setup instructions.
- **Tests**

items.title: docs: document runtime container memory profiles (SWR-G032)

labels.name: intent-target
labels.description: Intent automation target — implementation worker may claim this issue.

labels.name: intent-pr-approved
labels.description: PR is approved by intent automation review; ready to merge + close out.

items.body:
## Summary

Documents small / standard / large memory profiles for the local runtime container and explains the runtime settings that affect memory use. Documentation only.

## What changed

- **`docs/runtime-memory-profiles.md`** (new):
  - **Three profiles** — small (~512 MB), standard (~1–2 GB), large (~4 GB+) — with a starting container-memory limit and suggested settings each.
  - **How runtime memory is spent**: events are external; Orleans runs in-memory; the dominant inner cost is projection WASM (~36 MB per active instance), so memory ≈ `active projectors × SEKIBAN_WASM_POOL_SIZE × ~36 MB` + base process + accumulating in-memory projection state.
  - **Inner controls**: `SEKIBAN_PROJECTION_MODE` (dual / memory-only / materialized-view-only), `SEKIBAN_WASM_POOL_SIZE`, `SEKIBAN_WASMTIME_STATIC_MEMORY_MAX_MB`, `KEEP_TAG_PROJECTORS` — with their tradeoffs.
  - **Memory-limit examples**: `docker run --memory=1g …` and Compose `mem_limit`.
  - **Observing memory**: `GET /api/sekiban/memory-stats` (`{ processRssMB, projectors[] }`).
  - Explicit note that benchmark numbers are **observations, not guarantees** (links `docs/benchmark-results.md`).
- **`docker/sekiban-wasm-runtime/README.md`**: new "Memory Profiles" section + `SEKIBAN_WASMTIME_STATIC_MEMORY_MAX_MB` in the optional env-var table.
- **`README.md`**: pointer to the memory-profiles guide.

## Acceptance criteria

- ✅ Three memory profiles.
- ✅ Command/compose examples for memory limits.
- ✅ Explains projection mode and pool size tradeoffs.
- ✅ States benchmark numbers are observations, not guarantees.
- ✅ `git diff --check` passes.

## Verification

```bash
rg -n "small|standard|large|SEKIBAN_PROJECTION_MODE|SEKIBAN_WASM_POOL_SIZE|memory-stats|benchmark" docs README.md docker
git diff --check
```

All required tokens present across the updated docs; `git diff --check` clean. Docs-only change (no runtime behavior change).

Closes #177

5.6.0
=====

:release-date: 2025-11-30
:release-by: Tomer Nosrati

Celery v5.6.0 is now available.

Key Highlights
```

See :ref:`whatsnew-5.6` for a complete overview or read the main highlights below.

## Python 3.9 Minimum Version

Celery 5.6.0 drops support for Python 3.8 (EOL). The minimum required Python
version is now 3.9. Users still on Python 3.8 must upgrade their Python version
before upgrading to Celery 5.6.0.

Additionally, this release includes initial support for Python 3.14.

## SQS: Reverted to `pycurl` from `urllib3`

The switch from `pycurl` to `urllib3` for the SQS transport (introduced in
Celery 5.5.0 via Kombu) has been reverted due to critical issues affecting SQS
users:

- Processing throughput dropped from \~100 tasks/sec to \~3/sec in some environments
- `UnknownOperationException` errors causing container crash loops
- Silent message processing failures with no error logs

Users of the SQS transport must ensure `pycurl` is installed. If you removed
`pycurl` after upgrading to Celery 5.5.0, you will need to reinstall it.

Contributed by `@auvipy <https://github.com/auvipy>`\_ in
`#​9620 <https://github.com/celery/celery/pull/9620>`\_.

## Security Fix: Broker Credential Leak Prevention

Fixed a security issue where broker URLs containing passwords were being logged
in plaintext by the delayed delivery mechanism. Broker credentials are now
properly sanitized in all log output.

Contributed by `@giancarloromeo <https://github.com/giancarloromeo>`\_ in
`#​9997 <https://github.com/celery/celery/pull/9997>`\_.

## Memory Leak Fixes

Two significant memory leaks have been fixed in this release:

**Exception Handling Memory Leak**: Fixed a critical memory leak in task exception
handling that was particularly severe on Python 3.11+ due to enhanced traceback
data. The fix properly breaks reference cycles in tracebacks to allow garbage
collection.

Contributed by `@jaiganeshs21 <https://github.com/jaiganeshs21>`\_ in
`#​9799 <https://github.com/celery/celery/pull/9799>`\_.

**Pending Result Memory Leak**: Fixed a memory leak where `AsyncResult`
subscriptions were not being cleaned up when results were forgotten.

Contributed by `@tsoos99dev <https://github.com/tsoos99dev>`\_ in
`#​9806 <https://github.com/celery/celery/pull/9806>`\_.

## ETA Task Memory Limit

New configuration option :setting:`worker_eta_task_limit` to prevent out-of-memory
crashes when workers fetch large numbers of ETA or countdown tasks. Previously,
workers could exhaust available memory when the broker contained many scheduled tasks.

Example usage:

.. code-block:: python

```
app.conf.worker_eta_task_limit = 1000
```

Contributed by `@sashu2310 <https://github.com/sashu2310>`\_ in
`#​9853 <https://github.com/celery/celery/pull/9853>`\_.

## Queue Type Selection for Auto-created Queues

New configuration options allow specifying the queue type and exchange type when
Celery auto-creates missing queues. This is particularly useful for RabbitMQ users
who want to use quorum queues with auto-created queues.

Configuration options:

- :setting:`task_create_missing_queue_type`: Sets the queue type for auto-created
  queues (e.g., `quorum`, `classic`)
- :setting:`task_create_missing_queue_exchange_type`: Sets the exchange type for
  auto-created queues

Example usage:

.. code-block:: python

```
app.conf.task_create_missing_queue_type = 'quorum'
```

Contributed by `@ghirailghiro <https://github.com/ghirailghiro>`\_ in
`#​9815 <https://github.com/celery/celery/pull/9815>`\_.

Celery v5.5.0 is now available.

Key Highlights

```

See :ref:`whatsnew-5.5` for a complete overview or read the main highlights below.

Redis Broker Stability Improvements
-----------------------------------

Long-standing disconnection issues with the Redis broker have been identified and
resolved in Kombu 5.5.0, which is included with this release. These improvements
significantly enhance stability when using Redis as a broker.

Additionally, the Redis backend now has better exception handling with the new
``exception_safe_to_retry`` feature, which improves resilience during temporary
Redis connection issues. See :ref:`conf-redis-result-backend` for complete
documentation.

Contributed by `@drienkop <https://github.com/drienkop>`_ in
`#​9614 <https://github.com/celery/celery/pull/9614>`_.

``pycurl`` replaced with ``urllib3``
------------------------------------

Replaced the :pypi:`pycurl` dependency with :pypi:`urllib3`.

We're monitoring the performance impact of this change and welcome feedback from users
who notice any significant differences in their environments.

Contributed by `@spawn-guy <https://github.com/spawn-guy>`_ in Kombu
`#​2134 <https://github.com/celery/kombu/pull/2134>`_ and integrated in Celery via
`#​9526 <https://github.com/celery/celery/pull/9526>`_.

RabbitMQ Quorum Queues Support
------------------------------

Added support for RabbitMQ's new `Quorum Queues <https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/quorum-queues>`_
feature, including compatibility with ETA tasks. This implementation has some limitations compared
to classic queues, so please refer to the documentation for details.

`Native Delayed Delivery <https://docs.particular.net/transports/rabbitmq/delayed-delivery>`_
is automatically enabled when quorum queues are detected to implement the ETA mechanism.

See :ref:`using-quorum-queues` for complete documentation.

Configuration options:

- :setting:`broker_native_delayed_delivery_queue_type`: Specifies the queue type for
  delayed delivery (default: ``quorum``)
- :setting:`task_default_queue_type`: Sets the default queue type for tasks
  (default: ``classic``)
- :setting:`worker_detect_quorum_queues`: Controls automatic detection of quorum
  queues (default: ``True``)

`#​9121 <https://github.com/celery/celery/pull/9121>`_, and

For details regarding the 404 errors, see
`New Year's Security Incident <https://github.com/celery/celery/discussions/9525>`_.

Soft Shutdown Mechanism
-----------------------

Soft shutdown is a time limited warm shutdown, initiated just before the cold shutdown.
The worker will allow :setting:`worker_soft_shutdown_timeout` seconds for all currently
executing tasks to finish before it terminates. If the time limit is reached, the worker
will initiate a cold shutdown and cancel all currently executing tasks.

This feature is particularly valuable when using brokers with visibility timeout
mechanisms, such as Redis or SQS. It allows the worker enough time to re-queue
tasks that were not completed before exiting, preventing task loss during worker
shutdown.

See :ref:`worker-stopping` for complete documentation on worker shutdown types.

Configuration options:

- :setting:`worker_soft_shutdown_timeout`: Sets the duration in seconds for the soft
  shutdown period (default: ``0.0``, disabled)
- :setting:`worker_enable_soft_shutdown_on_idle`: Controls whether soft shutdown
  should be enabled even when the worker is idle (default: ``False``)

Contributed by `@Nusnus <https://github.com/Nusnus>`_ in
`#​9213 <https://github.com/celery/celery/pull/9213>`_,
`#​9231 <https://github.com/celery/celery/pull/9231>`_, and
`#​9238 <https://github.com/celery/celery/pull/9238>`_.

Pydantic Support
----------------

New native support for Pydantic models in tasks. This integration
allows you to leverage Pydantic's powerful data validation and serialization
capabilities directly in your Celery tasks.

Example usage:

.. code-block:: python

    from pydantic import BaseModel
    from celery import Celery

    app = Celery('tasks')

    class ArgModel(BaseModel):
        value: int

    class ReturnModel(BaseModel):
        value: str

    @​app.task(pydantic=True)
    def x(arg: ArgModel) -> ReturnModel:

### args/kwargs type hinted as Pydantic model will be converted
        assert isinstance(arg, ArgModel)

### The returned model will be converted to a dict automatically
        return ReturnModel(value=f"example: {arg.value}")

See :ref:`task-pydantic` for complete documentation.

Configuration options:

- ``pydantic=True``: Enables Pydantic integration for the task
- ``pydantic_strict=True/False``: Controls whether strict validation is enabled
  (default: ``False``)
- ``pydantic_context={...}``: Provides additional context for validation
- ``pydantic_dump_kwargs={...}``: Customizes serialization behavior

Contributed by `@mathiasertl <https://github.com/mathiasertl>`_ in
`#​9023 <https://github.com/celery/celery/pull/9023>`_,
`#​9319 <https://github.com/celery/celery/pull/9319>`_, and
`#​9393 <https://github.com/celery/celery/pull/9393>`_.

Google Pub/Sub Transport
------------------------

New support for Google Cloud Pub/Sub as a message transport, expanding
Celery's cloud integration options.

See :ref:`broker-gcpubsub` for complete documentation.

For the Google Pub/Sub support you have to install additional dependencies:

.. code-block:: console

    $ pip install "celery[gcpubsub]"

Then configure your Celery application to use the Google Pub/Sub transport:

.. code-block:: python

    broker_url = 'gcpubsub://projects/project-id'

Contributed by `@haimjether <https://github.com/haimjether>`_ in
`#​9351 <https://github.com/celery/celery/pull/9351>`_.

Python 3.13 Support
-------------------

Official support for Python 3.13. All core dependencies have been
updated to ensure compatibility, including Kombu and py-amqp.

This release maintains compatibility with Python 3.8 through 3.13, as well as
PyPy 3.10+.

Contributed by `@Nusnus <https://github.com/Nusnus>`_ in
`#​9309 <https://github.com/celery/celery/pull/9309>`_ and
`#​9350 <https://github.com/celery/celery/pull/9350>`_.

REMAP_SIGTERM Support
---------------------

The "REMAP_SIGTERM" feature, previously undocumented, has been tested, documented,
and is now officially supported. This feature allows you to remap the SIGTERM
signal to SIGQUIT, enabling you to initiate a soft or cold shutdown using TERM
instead of QUIT.

This is particularly useful in containerized environments where SIGTERM is the
standard signal for graceful termination.

See :ref:`Cold Shutdown documentation <worker-REMAP_SIGTERM>` for more info.

To enable this feature, set the environment variable:

.. code-block:: bash

    export REMAP_SIGTERM="SIGQUIT"

Contributed by `@Nusnus <https://github.com/Nusnus>`_ in
`#​9461 <https://github.com/celery/celery/pull/9461>`_.

Database Backend Improvements
-----------------------------

New ``create_tables_at_setup`` option for the database
backend. This option controls when database tables are created, allowing for
non-lazy table creation.

By default (``create_tables_at_setup=True``), tables are created during backend
initialization. Setting this to ``False`` defers table creation until they are
actually needed, which can be useful in certain deployment scenarios where you want
more control over database schema management.

See :ref:`conf-database-result-backend` for complete documentation.

Configuration:

.. code-block:: python

    app.conf.result_backend = 'db+sqlite:///results.db'
    app.conf.database_create_tables_at_setup = False

Contributed by `@MarcBresson <https://github.com/MarcBresson>`_ in
`#​9228 <https://github.com/celery/celery/pull/9228>`_.

items.title: feat: link Cedar policy templates on the PolicySet handle
items.body:
## Summary

Surfaces Cedar **policy templates** (policies with `?principal` / `?resource` slots) on the reusable `PolicySet` handle, extending the handle pattern from #91/#95 to template linking. `PolicySet.from_str` already parses templates; they just authorize nothing until linked. This adds the full linking lifecycle, immutable like the rest of the handle — every method returns a **new** `PolicySet`:

- `policy_set.with_linked_batch(links) -> PolicySet` — the primary path: clone the base once, apply every link, return a new handle. All-or-nothing (any failure raises, no handle returned).
- `policy_set.with_linked(template_id, new_id, values) -> PolicySet` — single-link convenience over the batch path.
- `policy_set.templates() -> list[dict]` — introspection: one dict per template with its `id`, `id_annotation` (the `@id`), `slots`, and the `links` derived from it (each link's `id` and bound `values`).
- `policy_set.without_linked(link_id) -> PolicySet` — a new handle with one linked policy removed.

A linked `PolicySet` is still just a `PolicySet`, so it evaluates through `is_authorized`, `is_authorized_batch`, and `is_authorized_partial` with no other changes. Existing callers are untouched — pure, opt-in addition.

Implements the template-linked policy support discussed in #29. (Happy to close #29 on merge, or leave it open if you'd rather keep tracking the other items from the thread — your call.)

> ### 📖 Please read the README "Linking policy templates" section first
> The [README section](README.md#linking-policy-templates) is the canonical reference for this change and intentionally covers a lot: the linking mechanics, the **`@id`-as-stable-key** reasoning (and why the positional `policy0` id is the fragile one), what a linked policy's `id` vs `@id` are, the `templates()` shape, and an honest **"should you reach for templates?"** efficiency discussion. The design-decision and performance notes below summarize it, but the README is where the reasoning lives.

## Motivation

Templates are Cedar's first-class, GA mechanism for **per-principal and per-resource grants** — "allow this person to view this photo while their subscription is active" — authored once and linked per grant, instead of an N-near-identical-policies string-concatenation. Two concrete consumers drove the shape (see #29): per-user permission grants in my own app, and the canonical per-principal sharing / multi-tenancy pattern templates were designed for. The crate already exposes everything needed (`PolicySet::link` / `unlink` / `templates` / `get_linked_policies`); the gap was a Python surface, which this fills following the immutable-handle precedent.

## Usage

```python
from cedarpy import PolicySet, is_authorized, Decision

# one rule: a subscriber may view a photo that's been granted to them
base = PolicySet.from_str(
    '@id("photo-access")\n'
    'permit(principal == ?principal, action == Action::"view", resource == ?resource)\n'
    'when { principal.subscriptionActive };'
)

# fill the slots to grant alice access to one photo
linked = base.with_linked(
    template_id="photo-access",
    new_id="alice-vacation",
    values={"?principal": 'User::"alice"', "?resource": 'Photo::"vacation.jpg"'},
)

entities = [{"uid": {"type": "User", "id": "alice"},
             "attrs": {"subscriptionActive": True}, "parents": []}]
request = {"principal": 'User::"alice"', "action": 'Action::"view"', "resource": 'Photo::"vacation.jpg"'}

result = is_authorized(request, linked, entities)
assert result.decision == Decision.Allow
result.diagnostics.reasons                    # ['alice-vacation']  (the link's id)
result.diagnostics.id_annotations_by_reason   # {'alice-vacation': 'photo-access'}  (inherited @id)
```

```python
# grant many at once — with_linked_batch clones the base once and applies every link
linked = base.with_linked_batch([
    {"template_id": "photo-access", "new_id": "alice-vacation",
     "values": {"?principal": 'User::"alice"', "?resource": 'Photo::"vacation.jpg"'}},
    {"template_id": "photo-access", "new_id": "bob-skyline",
     "values": {"?principal": {"type": "User", "id": "bob"}, "?resource": 'Photo::"skyline.jpg"'}},
])
```

Slot values accept a Cedar string (`'User::"jane"'`) or a `{"type","id"}` dict — the same two forms a request principal/resource already accepts (#87).

## Design decisions

- **Mirror the immutable-handle precedent (#91/#95).** Cedar's `link`/`unlink` mutate a `PolicySet`; cedarpy clones the base and returns a **new** handle, so a single compiled base is shared across threads/requests without a clone-before-mutate footgun. Every mutating-sounding method (`with_linked`, `with_linked_batch`, `without_linked`) returns a new handle.
- **`with_linked_batch` is primary; `with_linked` is sugar.** Per the #29 discussion, the batch path is the real primitive: it clones the base **once** and applies all links (one clone per batch, not per link), and it's all-or-nothing. `with_linked` delegates to it. The `_batch` suffix mirrors the repo's own `is_authorized` / `is_authorized_batch` convention.
- **Identify templates by `@id`, not the positional id.** A `template_id` resolves to a template's literal Cedar id first, then to its `@id` annotation value (the labeling convention the Cedar CLI's `link` uses; `@id` is otherwise inert, per the repo's #66/#68/#74/#77 history). **Prefer the `@id`:** the positional id (`policy0`, …) is reassigned per parse and renumbered by `with_added_str`, while the `@id` is invariant. Resolution never renames or rebuilds the set, and the `@id` match must be unambiguous. Resolution is **indexed once per batch** (`build_template_id_index`), so a batch of `L` links over `T` templates is `O(T + L)`, not `O(T × L)`; the raw-`&str` annotation scan avoids Cedar's identifier-parse cost (same pattern as `lookup_id_annotation`).
- **`new_id` matches Cedar's naming across surfaces.** The link-spec keys `template_id` / `new_id` / `values` are the snake_case of Cedar's own: Rust `PolicySet::link(template_id, new_id, vals)`, CLI `--template-id` / `--new-id`, and the EST/JSON `templateId` / `newId` / `values`. `new_id` is the id of the new template-linked policy (the filled-in slots, which evaluate as a policy) — neither a template id nor a principal.
- **`templates()` is the one introspection call.** It returns the template definition *and* the links nested under each template (each link's `id` and bound `values`), composed from `templates()` / `Template::slots()`/`annotations()` / `get_linked_policies` / `template_links()`. A linked policy's id is its `new_id` (what `reasons` reports); its `@id` is inherited from the template.
- **Refactor: shared entity-uid extraction.** `extract_euid_field` (request principals) and slot-value parsing now share `euid_input_from_value`, with the error label computed lazily (a closure) so the hot success path allocates no label — request error messages are byte-identical.

## Behavior changes

None for existing callers. Purely additive: a `PolicySet` may now contain template-linked policies, and the new methods are opt-in. No new metrics, no new Cargo feature — regular template linking works on the pinned engine (4.8.2).

## Performance

**Authorization hot path: neutral.** A linked `PolicySet` evaluates exactly like a static one; the only `is_authorized`-path change is the `euid_input_from_value` refactor, which is allocation-free on the success path.

**Build cost (the interesting axis), and an honest one — this is *not* a general speedup.** A quick build benchmark (not committed; see "Should you reach for templates?" in the README) of generating + parsing N policies vs one template + N links via `with_linked_batch`, at N=200 grants:

| policy body | build speed | memory | winner |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 condition (subscription) | 0.7× | 1.0× | generate+parse |
| ~4 conditions | 1.2× | 1.8× | ~parity |
| ~10 conditions (realistic rich) | **~2×** | **~2.5×** | templates |

(speed/mem = generate+parse ÷ template; >1 favors templates.) Templates pay off as the policy body gets heavier — the rule is parsed and held *once* and shared across links instead of copied per grant — and are slightly *worse* for trivial policies (the per-link binding exceeds a tiny static policy). For typical/basic policies it's roughly a wash; the README says so plainly and tells readers to profile their own shapes.

## Test plan

- [x] `maturin develop --release` — clean build, no warnings
- [x] `pytest tests/unit` — **198 passed** (+42 new in `tests/unit/test_template_linking.py`: parse/round-trip, single + batch link evaluation through `is_authorized`/`_batch`/`_partial`, immutability, batch clone-once + all-or-nothing atomicity (incl. intra-batch duplicate `new_id`), both slot-value forms, `?principal`/`?resource`/both slots, `@id`-vs-literal resolution + ambiguity, `templates()` shape incl. nested links, `without_linked` + relink, schema compose, shared-handle-across-threads, and an **upstream-anchored round-trip over Cedar's own `sandbox_c` sample**, vendored under `tests/unit/resources/sandbox_c/` with provenance)
- [x] `pyright` clean for the changed surface (`cedarpy/_internal.pyi` updated)
- [x] `make integration-tests` — **74 passed**
- [x] `make benchmark-compare` — **performance-neutral.** The gate reports `test_simple_policy_allow`/`_deny` over the 5% threshold (+5.5% / +5.6%), but this is `baseline.json` drift + warm-machine noise, not this change: the whole suite is uniformly elevated (+1–5.5%, including benchmarks this PR doesn't touch, e.g. `test_small_entity_set` +4.8%), the two flagged benchmarks are the trivial-policy authz path (unchanged here bar the allocation-free `euid_input_from_value` refactor), and a HEAD-vs-`main` A/B confirmed `main` itself trips the gate on this machine — the same `baseline.json`-predates-many-merged-commits drift noted in #91/#95. New template benchmarks have no baseline and are skipped.

## Questions for review

- **Tracked benchmark?** The README cites build-time + memory numbers from a quick ad-hoc benchmark (worded as such, not committed). Happy to add a committed, reproducible template build+memory benchmark under `tests/benchmark/` if you'd like — it'd be a standalone script, *not* through the median-of-N authz regression gate (it's build/memory, not authz timing).
- **Leveraging upstream test data:** this vendors Cedar's `sandbox_c` and reproduces its documented `link` walkthrough; happy to pull in more cedar-policy / cedar-java template fixtures if you want broader coverage (per your note in #29).

---

*Implementation assisted by AI tooling; design decisions, testing strategy, and code review performed by the author.*

items.title: chore(agents): 10-agent SDLC team with a handshake protocol
items.body:
## What

Reshapes `.claude/agents/` from an ad-hoc set into a complete **10-agent SDLC team**, one clear owner per phase, with a shared **handshake-file** context protocol and **anti-hallucination** grounding rules across every agent.

## Roster (exactly 10, one per SDLC phase)

| # | Agent | Phase | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `orchestrator` | Lead / delivery (owns the handshake) | updated |
| 2 | `backlog-agent` | Requirements | updated |
| 3 | `architect` | Architecture / technical design, contracts, ADRs | **new** |
| 4 | `ux-designer` | UX design | updated |
| 5 | `schema-agent` | Data & tenancy | updated |
| 6 | `service-builder` | Backend | updated |
| 7 | `frontend-dev` | Frontend | updated |
| 8 | `qa-agent` | Test & reliability (suite + RCA) | **new** — absorbs `verify` + `rca-agent` |
| 9 | `security-agent` | Security & DoD gate | **new** — absorbs `review-agent` |
| 10 | `docs-agent` | Documentation | updated |

Removed standalone `verify`, `rca-agent`, `review-agent` (their duties merged into `qa-agent` / `security-agent`).

## The handshake protocol (minimizes hallucination)

Subagents are stateless, so each task gets one source-of-truth file the team reads and updates as work flows through the SDLC.

- `.claude/agents/handshake.template.md` — structured template: task/issue, verbatim acceptance criteria, per-stage status matrix, decisions & contracts, real verification output, open questions, append-only hand-off log.
- `.claude/handshakes/<branch>.md` — created per task by the orchestrator; **git-ignored** (only the dir README is tracked).
- Every agent **reads it before acting** and **updates its own section on hand-off**; no agent deletes another's section; **source wins** on conflict.

## Anti-hallucination rules (in every agent)

1. Facts come from source, not memory — cite `file:line`.
2. Never fabricate issue numbers / table-columns / routes / file paths / test counts — mark `UNKNOWN` and get it from the owner.
3. Verify before you claim — done/passing needs real pasted output.
4. Reuse before invent; stay in your lane (delegate the rest).

## Also updated for consistency

- `.claude/agents/README.md` — new roster table, SDLC flow diagram, handshake + anti-hallucination sections.
- `AGENTS.md` §5 — roles table + hand-off protocol now reference the handshake.
- `CLAUDE.md` — routing list, RCA → `qa-agent`, DoD sign-off → `security-agent`.
- `.gitignore` — ignore live handshakes, keep the README.

## Notes

- Docs/config only — no application code, schema, or RLS touched.
- Verified: roster is exactly 10, every agent references the handshake, and there are zero dangling references to the removed agents.
- Reload via `/agents` (or a new session) for Claude Code to pick up the new specs.
